2026-08-03: Census reported US June 2026 total construction spending at USD 2,166.5 billion and nonresidential at USD 745.3 billion (both seasonally adjusted annual rates).
outlook: For 2026–2027, expect a low-growth, disciplined market: demand holds in sectors tied to domestic fabrication, industrial production, and nonresidential infrastructure, while regulatory spend and chemical/process compliance reduce free margin. A likely 2027 baseline is modest growth, but operators that invest in PFAS-compliant treatment, process digitalization, and high-spec aerospace/defense capabilities should outperform.

Downstream outsourcing: downstream manufacturers continue to use specialized platers for quality, compliance, and flexibility
Low consolidation threshold: fragmented operator base with periodic consolidators
Industrial resilience over expansion: demand tied to manufacturing mix rather than broad consumer cycles
Cost-volatility management: materials and compliance costs drive process and pricing discipline
one_sentence: US demand in 2025–2026 is stabilizing from construction and manufacturing activity while PFAS-focused wastewater regulation raises cost and complexity for job-shop operators.

title: Metal Stamping & Forging in the US
one_liner: U.S. metal stamping and forging is shifting toward higher-value aerospace, defense, and industrial applications as trade policy raises local sourcing pressure and drives consolidation.
overview: The US market is currently re-anchoring around mission-critical end markets rather than mass-commodity stamping and forging. Trade action under Section 232 has increased domestic manufacturing relevance for steel-intensive parts, while aerospace demand indicators and defense spending posture continue to support capacity utilization and selective premium pricing. Independent industry trackers also show stronger financial and valuation momentum in the forging and stamping segment during early 2026, even as parts of supply chains face import-policy and cost volatility.

title: Metal Tank Manufacturing in the US

Recent energy-market signals in 2025–26 show both stabilization and volatility: fuel flows and exports remain large but uneven by destination, while domestic tank fabrication demand is still supported by petrochemical, utility, refinery and agriculture users needing storage and process-vessel capacity. Recent operator disclosures also show consolidation and portfolio moves to expand capabilities in tank servicing, pressure components, and custom welding/fabrication.

Order flow in some downstream sectors is uneven year-on-year as broader manufacturing and construction activity has been volatile.
Domestic steel-related cost volatility and tariff/compliance exposure continue to pressure margins for smaller custom manufacturers.

2025-06-20: LT Corporation completed acquisition of Tanco Engineering for national expansion in welded steel storage-tank construction and service,
2025-05-07: TF Warren Group acquired KEMCO (Krueger Engineering and Manufacturing), adding shell and tube heat-exchanger-related heavy-fabrication capacity in Houston,
2026-03-10: EIA reported U.S. crude oil exports down 3% in 2025; exports shifted in composition as regions adjusted despite strong underlying production,
2025-10-07: EIA reported U.S. propane inventories and production strength, with Gulf Coast inventories above five-year norms and production up 5% YTD.
outlook: Short-term growth is likely moderate: demand from energy logistics and chemical processing remains supportive, while steel-commodity costs, tariffs, and labor pressure constrain margin expansion; players with stronger service portfolios, MRO capabilities, and NAICS-specified custom engineering depth should outperform.
themes: Energy-linked demand concentration remains the key cyclical driver
Import substitution and tariff policy increase the relative importance of domestic fabrication and repair capability
Consolidation continues via bolt-on acquisitions to build turnkey service breadth
Margin leadership increasingly depends on lifecycle service revenue and installation/field-erection capabilities
Raw-material and compliance risk management is becoming a core competitive differentiator
Localized manufacturing resilience in logistics/energy clusters matters more than broad capacity growth
one_sentence: US metal tank manufacturing remains a niche but strategic fabrication segment where demand tracks energy and industrial-cycle spending, while domestic sourcing pressure rises as steel import volumes weaken and supplier costs stay elevated.

title: Metal Wholesaling in the US
one_liner: US metal wholesalers sit between primary metal producers and manufacturers/construction users, with revenue sensitive to steel and nonferrous price cycles and demand from industrial production.
overview: Metal and mineral merchant wholesalers in NAICS 4235 distribute iron, steel, aluminum, and nonferrous products across manufacturing, construction, and heavy industrial end-markets. Industry economics remain highly cyclical: volume moves with industrial activity and metal-price inflation, while profitability depends on scale, local fulfillment capability, and value-added processing.

market_size.unit: BLS/FRED sectoral output, Millions of Dollars, not seasonally adjusted

baseline_2022.growth: −2.25% projected CAGR for 2022-2028 (IBIS baseline outlook); 2003-2022 market-size CAGR 1.20%

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is generated by buying primary metals from mills, holding inventories, applying handling and value-added services (cutting, sawing, finishing, packaging, special order processing), and reselling into fabrication, construction, utilities, and industrial accounts with short lead times and custom order sizes.

primary_costs: Purchase cost of metals (mainly steel/aluminum and nonferrous inventories)
Inventory carrying cost and obsolescence risk when commodity prices fall
Logistics and distribution costs (warehousing, handling, last-mile delivery)
Labor and overhead in service and processing operations
margin_drivers: Ability to pass through metal price moves with limited lag
Share of sales from value-added processing vs pure transaction wholesaling
Asset utilization at facilities and regional network density

2025: MWTS (U.S. Census) shows NAICS 4235 monthly sales volatility; May 2025 metals wholesaling sales were negative versus prior year in that month, while sales-to-date were slightly positive.
2025: Industrial activity is mixed at the margin; Federal Reserve G.17 indicates IP was up but manufacturing was flat in Nov 2025, while total industrial production rose versus a year earlier.
2026: BLS PPI indicates steel mill products inflation remains elevated in June 2026, reinforcing input cost pressure for wholesalers carrying metal inventories.
2026: Consolidation theme persists, with large service-center operators expanding footprint and processing capabilities despite fragmented local competition.
whats_growing: Value-added services (processing + fast-turn delivery), which reduce direct price exposure on base commodity transactions.
Scale advantages from larger regional networks that improve service reliability and inventory turn.
Consolidation of niche and smaller operators into larger platforms.
whats_shrinking: Transaction-only wholesalers under price stress from commodity volatility and tight conversion margins.
Industry-level tonnage/volume, which remains challenged (MSCI-reported sector volume decline of around 1.0% in 2025).
Purely ad-hoc pricing power as buyers push for predictable pricing from distributors amid volatility.
recent_developments: 2025-05: U.S. Census MWTS for NAICS 4235 shows metals monthly sales weaker than prior year (May year-on-year negative), while monthly YTD remained slightly positive.
2025-11: Federal Reserve G.17 release reports Nov 2025 total industrial production up and manufacturing flat, affecting metals-demand direction but not strongly bullish.
2025-12-31: Reliance reported $14.29bn 2025 net sales and said its U.S. tons sold were about 17% of industry tonnage, up from ~15% in 2024 (highly fragmented market context).
2026-01: Ryerson reported the post-quarter Olympic Steel merger, positioning as North America’s second-largest metals service center.
2026-06: BLS PPI June release shows steel mill products up 3.6% and states final-demand goods remained volatile, supporting a cautious procurement posture.
outlook: Expect flat-to-low single-digit revenue changes in 2026 with continued dependence on manufacturing and construction cycles, broad industry consolidation, and stronger emphasis on value-added processing to defend margins during metal-price swings; demand quality likely diverges by region and vertical.
themes: Consolidation among large service centers
Inventory and pricing risk management
Value-added processing differentiation
Domestic sourcing and mill-to-service-center relationship leverage
Regional competitive fragmentation despite national leaders
one_sentence: The industry remains fragmented by geography but increasingly favors large metal service centers that bundle inventory availability, processing, and fast delivery to manage volatile input costs and margin pressure.

title: Metalworking Machinery Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: The US metalworking machinery industry is a cyclical, capital-intensive producer of CNC and conventional tooling machinery showing a mixed 2025-2026 recovery in output and orders but weak labor-force expansion.
overview: Metalworking machinery makers produce machines and tooling used to shape, cut, form, and finish metal parts, including special dies, jigs, fixtures, and accessories. The segment is downstream of manufacturing, mining, energy, and defense supply chains and is sensitive to capex cycles, trade conditions, and skilled-labor costs. In the latest cycle, survey-based order series indicate renewed demand for productivity upgrades, while official employment and compensation data show a softer structural job trend.
how_it_makes_money: Revenue is earned from sales of metalworking machine tools, machine accessories, cutting systems, industrial molds, special tooling fixtures, and rolling/folding/forming platforms; manufacturers also monetize installation, retrofits, remote diagnostics, tooling integration, service agreements, and spare parts.

key_cost_drivers: financing and working-capital costs during long project cycles
cost_structure.price_risk: Export-price index for NAICS 3335 was 153.4 in Sep/Oct 2025 and 152.1 in Dec 2025, signaling limited easing in export pricing pressure in late 2025.

current_dynamics: Demand is rebounding unevenly: AMT’s USMTO series shows a sharp short-term order pickup into Q1 2026, while official BLS-based NAICS 3335 figures show only partial recovery in sectoral output with declining 2025 employment. Order activity is increasingly supported by automation and resilience spending in sectors facing workforce shortages and higher skill costs.
whats_growing: Q1 2026 machine-tech demand: AMT reported national metalworking machinery orders of $681.3 million in Mar 2026 (+40.3% vs Feb; +31.5% vs Mar 2025).
2026 USMTO Q1 total of $1.61 billion (+27.8% YoY), indicating stronger near-term capex sentiment.
Higher-value automation and digital-retrofit spending where buyers avoid full machine replacement.
whats_shrinking: NAICS 3335 employment declined to 151.9k in 2025 from 156.8k in 2024.
Labor compensation trend in official NAICS 3335 series declined modestly in 2025, indicating near-term margin tightening risk.
Demand in some subsegments remains weaker in contract machine shops versus broader manufacturing-tech demand.
recent_developments: 2026-05-11: AMT reported Mar 2026 metalworking machinery orders of $681.3M, +40.3% from Feb 2026 and +31.5% YoY (USMTO).
2025-11-28: AMT/MTA reported first 9 months of 2025 machine-tool orders at $3,933M, +18% YoY on rolling 9M basis.

2026-06-29: FRED showed NAICS 3335 sectoral output at 32,210.183 million USD for 2025.
2026-06-04: FRED showed June 2026 metalworking machinery new orders at 3,024 million USD.
outlook: 2026 is likely to remain mixed: headline order momentum is strong, but the sector continues to run against a slower employment base and disciplined capex budgets from parts of the industrial base. US demand should stay positive where automation, defense, data-center power, and aerospace programs drive replacement cycles, while lower-priced and slower-technology demand pockets remain price sensitive.
themes: automation and labor shortage substitution
policy-driven capital spending in industrial corridors
high import price sensitivity and resilience-focused sourcing
defense/aerospace and energy-infrastructure demand spillover
service-led business models (software, monitoring, retrofit kits)
one_sentence: US NAICS 3335 data show modestly higher 2025 production and stronger 2026 machine-order momentum, while workforce levels remain below 2025/2024 levels and profit pressure remains tied to equipment, labor, and financing costs.

title: Methanol Production in the US
one_liner: U.S. methanol remains a gas-led, volatile commodity business where new Gulf Coast capacity offsets cyclical price swings from feedstock, outages, and freight dynamics.
overview: The U.S. methanol industry is a concentrated, capital-intensive chemicals segment with high dependence on natural gas as the primary feedstock. Production climbed from about 8.2 million metric tons (Mt) in 2022 and has been supported by new Gulf Coast and related expansions, while demand exposure remains split across chemical derivatives and fuel-related demand channels. Recent filings and company reports in 2025-2026 show stronger capacity utilization at key U.S. assets but also recurring downtime and gas-supply sensitivity, underscoring ongoing operating risk despite structural demand support.

key_stats.market_size: US$3,662 million (US industry revenue, 2022 baseline); Methanex Q2 2026 revenue US$1,395 million (company-level period value)
key_stats.growth: IBIS baseline: 9.40% CAGR 2003-2022; projected 2022-2028 CAGR -0.25%; operational expansion from 10.0 Mt capacity in 2022 to 13.5 Mt by end-2025
key_stats.capacity: U.S. projected methanol capacity reached 13.5 Mt by end-2025 (from 10.0 Mt in 2022)
key_stats.price: Methanex average realized methanol price in Q1 2026 was US$351/t and rose to US$529/t in Q2 2026

how_it_makes_money: Producers monetize methanol mostly through sale of bulk methanol for downstream derivatives (for example formaldehyde/acetic acid chain chemistry) and fuel/energy applications, using a mix of long-term offtake and spot-linked commercial terms. EBITDA is highly sensitive to realized methanol price and volume, with revenue tied to commodity cycles and plant uptime.

cost_structure.primary_input: Natural gas is the dominant feedstock, and higher gas and gas-linked contract components directly lift operating costs.
cost_structure.asset_availability: Plant outages, winter/summer gas-constrained operations, and turnaround activity create periodic output reductions and step-changes in unit cost.
cost_structure.logistics: Transportation, storage, and vessel routing materially affect delivered economics; shipping/handling cost pressure is noted in producer disclosures.
cost_structure.scale_and_mix: Higher share of internally produced methanol sales versus purchased methanol improves economics; geography/plant mix shifts affect transport costs and realized margin.

major_players: US Methanol LLC (including St. James Liberty One operations)
Koch Methanol (St. James / former YCI Methanol One)
current_dynamics: Feedstock-driven margin volatility is the core dynamic in 2025-2026: methanol plants reported quarter-to-quarter production swings, while market pricing improved significantly by mid-2026 from a low Q1 baseline. Integration-related execution (especially after the OCI acquisition) is actively shaping capacity use, product mix, and financing structure at leading producers. At the same time, low-carbon and marine-fuel narratives are expanding demand optionality, but operational reliability and gas access remain gating factors.
whats_growing: US methanol production capacity expansion through 2025 (including Geismar 3 and 2025 projects) increased industrial-scale ability to replace imported volumes.
U.S. demand channels tied to downstream chemicals and fuel transitions remain supportive versus the 2009-2022 long-term build.
Methanol as a marine fuel ecosystem continues to mature globally, supporting potential incremental demand pathways.
Capital discipline and integration activity have improved cash-generation focus at major listed producers.
whats_shrinking: Traditional reliance on imported methanol volumes from a narrow supplier set is structurally less dominant as domestic projects reach commercial output.
Unplanned production due to outages and gas disruptions has reduced quarterly output at key plants in 2026.
Gross margin quality is being pressured by realized-price volatility when benchmark prices weaken quarter to quarter.
recent_developments: 2025-06-27: Methanex completed the OCI Global methanol business acquisition.
2026-03-05: Methanex reported fourth quarter 2025 results with 2,689,000 t of total methanol sales and full-year 2025 production of 10,469,000 t.
2026-05-11: U.S. EIA reported record 2025 natural-gas and energy output, including 39 Tcf dry gas in 2025.
2026-07-28: Methanex reported Q2 2026 net income swing and methanol production of 2,213,000 t, with realized price rising to US$529/t from Q1.
2026-07-28: Methanex announced indefinite idling of the Titan plant and restructuring in Trinidad and Tobago.
outlook: Near-term direction is likely to remain mixed: structural expansion and demand diversification support a firmer utilization base, while price, gas-availability, and reliability risk keep the sector cyclical. 2026 filings suggest stronger margins can coexist with lower production at certain sites due to outages, so investors should monitor plant-level uptime and gas-supply discipline more than headline capacity growth alone.
themes: Feedstock-cost dominance (natural gas)
Domestic capacity addition versus import displacement
Marine and alternative-fuel demand in transport
Low-carbon methanol and renewables-linked portfolio repositioning
Cycle management through integration and asset-mix optimization
one_sentence: Capacity expansion through 2025 has strengthened U.S. supply flexibility, but production and margins stay highly sensitive to natural-gas-linked costs, with 2025-2026 data showing continued project-driven growth alongside supply interruptions.

title: Mexican Restaurants
one_liner: Mexican restaurants in the U.S. are in a moderate-growth phase, with chain-led fast-casual formats offsetting margin pressure from elevated labor and food input costs.
overview: The U.S. Mexican restaurant industry had rebuilt after the 2020 disruption and remained one of the stronger categories within restaurant dining by 2022, with revenue at USD 76.7bn and broad category growth outlook into the late 2020s. The latest public-company signals in 2025-2026 show mixed execution at chain level: Chipotle faced a sharp comps reset in early 2025, while Taco Bell and other high-scale Mexican brands continued to post strong same-store sales in 2026. Sector dynamics in 2026 emphasize value-driven demand, delivery/mobile ordering, faster unit-level technology adoption, and continued menu-led traffic support.

key_stats.market_size: USD 86.1bn (estimated 2026, derived from 2022 baseline of USD 76.7bn and IBISWorld 2.93% annualized trend)
key_stats.growth: Low-single-digit annualized growth in 2026 estimated from 2022–2028 IBISWorld trend
key_stats.establishments: about 68,200 (estimated 2026, from IBISWorld 2022 base of 61,581 and +2.58% annualized growth)
key_stats.profit_margin: mid-single-digit to low-double-digit at operator level, with Chipotle reporting 12.9% operating margin in 2026 Q1

how_it_makes_money.revenue_model: Primarily sale of dine-in, takeout, delivery, and drive-thru meals; mix increasingly influenced by repeatable fast-casual formats and higher-margin menu innovation.
how_it_makes_money.drivers: Unit expansion, transaction lift from menu rotations, digital ordering convenience, and higher basket sizes through beverages and cross-category add-ons.
how_it_makes_money.pricing_power: Constrained by value competition; operators increasingly rely on operational efficiency and limited price increases.
how_it_makes_money.channel_mix: Digital order channels remain critical; chip-based loyalty and app funnels are becoming core traffic and margin levers.

Demand still supports Mexican-format growth, but inflation-adjusted dining budgets are tighter, increasing emphasis on perceived value. High-performing operators are pushing digital convenience and repeatability over purely culinary breadth. Menu innovation around proteins, beverages, and limited-time offers remains a major lever.
whats_growing: Value-led fast-casual Mexican formats with stronger traffic efficiency and loyalty-led repeat behavior
Digital ordering and app-based loyalty channels, shown by rising digital mix for large operators
Beverage-led traffic strategies and combo/meal-program innovation to defend ticket quality
whats_shrinking: Comparable growth for at least one large Mexican chain in 2025 (Chipotle Q2 downturn showed pressure can occur quickly)
Unprofitable operator share is elevated in softer traffic periods, consistent with sector-level margin stress
Purely traditional models with weak automation and low digital penetration versus digitally integrated peers

outlook: The category is likely to remain a steady grower through 2026 as mainstream demand for Mexican flavors persists, but the distribution of gains will concentrate in operators that can manage cost leakage and keep value messaging strong. National operator economics indicate moderate industry expansion but continued volatility at store level.

value-led differentiation
digital ordering and operational analytics
labor inflation and workforce retention
menu innovation with Mexican authenticity plus localization

title: Midwives & Doulas
one_liner: Demand is being reshaped by Medicaid policy expansion and maternal-care access pressures, while overall birth volume remains slightly soft.
overview: The US market remains relatively small in share of maternity care but increasingly important as cost and access pressures grow. Midwives (including certified nurse-midwives and related pathways) and doulas now play a larger role in prenatal, labor, and early postpartum support, especially where Medicaid reimbursement and state-level policy support expansion. In 2025, total births remained below 2024 (provisional 2025 data), while cesarean rates remained elevated, reinforcing pressure for lower-intensity care models.
how_it_makes_money: Primary revenue is professional fee-for-service for prenatal, delivery, and postpartum support billed through Medicaid/CHIP and commercial insurance; in many states midwife claims are paid through state Medicaid fee schedules and bundled maternity payment arrangements. Doulas increasingly receive Medicaid reimbursement in more states, with paid service components including prenatal visits, labor-and-delivery support, and postpartum visits (including in-home or virtual support in some states).

major_costs: Clinician labor and staffing (CNMs, midwives, and support staff) as the dominant variable cost
State-specific credentialing, licensure compliance, and credential-eligibility workflow
Claims administration (NPI, managed care/facility contracts, prior authorization) due to Medicaid policy variation
cost_markers: Doula payment scopes in state Medicaid programs vary widely, with reported labor/delivery doula support around $459 to $1,500 in 2026 policy analyses
Full-time AMCB-certificants are concentrated in a $100,000-$149,999 annual income band, indicating labor intensity of service delivery models

major_players: National Association of Certified Professional Midwives (NACPM)
State Medicaid agencies and Medicaid managed care plans
Integrated health systems with certified midwife-led maternity services
current_dynamics: Coverage-policy momentum is strong, with more states bringing Medicaid-paid doula services into routine maternal benefits while AMCB-certified workforce and state licensing frameworks continue to mature. At the same time, birth-volume softness in 2025 and ongoing provider-shortage pressures keep utilization growth from accelerating across the entire industry.
whats_growing: 2025-2026: Medicaid doula coverage expanded to 26 states + DC, with 17 of these states adding 12-month postpartum doula eligibility.
Midwife workforce formalization remains visible; AMCB reports 14,540 certified CNMs/CMs as of 2025-01-23.
Medicaid model design is becoming broader (global maternity, blended FFS/MCO billing, quality/reporting integration).
whats_shrinking: 2025 provisional births fell to 3,606,400 from 3,628,934 in 2024 (-1.0%), weakening volume growth.
The general fertility rate declined to 53.1 in 2025 (from 53.8 in 2024).
Access constraints still vary by state: CPM recognition remains uneven (37 states licensed, 11 unlicensed/unregulated as of March 2025).
recent_developments: 2025-01-23: AMCB reported 14,540 certified midwives (14,401 CNMs and 139 CMs).
2025-03: NACPM state-recognition handout reported 37 states with CPM licensure, 11 unlicensed/unregulated, and 2 with legal status in flux.
2025-04-23: CDC press release on 2024 provisional births reported 3,622,673 births and general fertility 54.6.
2026-01-20: CMS maternal health page update highlighted >40% of births on Medicaid/CHIP and postpartum-model initiatives.
2026-03-01: NASHP doula tracking update notes 26 states + DC covering doula services under Medicaid.
2026-04-09: CDC provisional 2025 report showed births 3,606,400 and cesarean 32.5% (low-risk cesarean 26.9%).
outlook: Near term, policy expansion in Medicaid-supported doula and midwife services should keep the industry resilient despite a soft birth trend. Mid- to longer-term growth should be demand-driven by workforce-access constraints in obstetrics and by value-of-care initiatives; however, uneven state licensing and reimbursement systems will continue to segment service quality and scaling speed.
themes: Medicaid-led maternal support expansion
State-by-state licensing variance for CPM/CM pathways
Doula integration into value-oriented perinatal care bundles
Shift from physician-only birth models toward collaborative care
Rural access and perinatal outcomes as policy catalysts
one_sentence: US midwifery and doula services are shifting from niche add-ons toward mainstream maternity-care support, but policy fragmentation and slower birth growth remain constraints.

title: Millwork Product Wholesaling
one_liner: Millwork product wholesalers are stabilizing around value-added distribution and custom service as new-home momentum cools and remodeling demand stays resilient.
overview: The NAICS 4233 space (Lumber and Other Construction Materials Merchant Wholesalers, including millwork and related wood building components) has been driven by householding housing-cycle shifts and volatile commodity costs through 2025–26. Public and private operators reported consolidation and footprint expansion, especially in acquisition-led branches and service capabilities, while remaining sensitive to private residential construction and commodity input pricing.

key_stats.market_size: 188,100.5 (Million USD, 2025 annual, NAICS 4233 sectoral output)

how_it_makes_money: Distributes building products tied to construction demand, including lumber, sheet goods, windows, doors, and millwork.
Generates profit through product gross margin on distributed and value-added inventory mix.
Adds higher-margin services around planning, installation, turnkey framing, and shell construction.
Earns revenue from broader value-added categories (siding, exterior trim, structural components) and bundled distributor services.

cost_structure.raw_material_inputs: Significant exposure to lumber/panel costs and volatility, especially in engineered wood and structural categories.
cost_structure.transportation_logistics: Distribution, freight, and handling costs rise with volume and route complexity, pressing operating leverage.
cost_structure.services_and_labor: Turnkey and installation-led offerings increase labor intensity and service complexity but help preserve customer lock-in.

current_dynamics: New residential starts remain uneven: Census reported 1,427,000 housing starts in June 2026, slightly above June 2025, while residential construction spending stayed slightly softer at the monthly level. National Remodeling Index readings stayed above expansionary thresholds, supporting replacement/remodel demand. Industry leaders reported lower core sales in some 2025–26 periods as they partially offset demand softness with acquisitions and stronger specialty-mix execution.
whats_growing: 2026: remodeling demand remained positive, with NAHB RMI improving to 64 for Q4 2025 and 2025/2026 forecasts still showing expansion.
2026: SRS Distribution continued strategic M&A to expand branches and category mix, including LS Building Products and Sider Lumber in February 2026.
Specialty/turnkey products and services that combine millwork, installation, and design support remain structurally stronger than pure commodity lines.
whats_shrinking: 2026: Builders FirstSource reported Q2 2026 net sales down 8.8% year-over-year from a lower housing-starts environment.
2026: Commodity categories tied to new residential new-construction intensity faced pressure; lumber/panel price swings pressured structural margin structure.
2026: Construction spending in June remained below the prior year at total and private levels despite some nonresidential stabilization.
recent_developments: 2026-08-03: U.S. Census reported total U.S. construction spending at $2,166.5B SAAR in June 2026; private construction at $1,622.5B SAAR and nonresidential at $745.3B SAAR.
2026-06-30: Builders FirstSource reported Q2 2026 net sales of $3.9B, down 8.8% year-over-year, with lower housing starts cited as a main headwind.
2026-07-30: Builders FirstSource scheduled a conference call for Q2 2026 results and reiterated acquisition-led repositioning in turnkey millwork solutions.
2025-09-26: Builders FirstSource announced acquisitions in turnkey millwork (Builder’s Door & Trim and Rystin Construction) in the Las Vegas area.
2026-02-27: SRS Distribution acquired LS Building Products; its acquisition list also includes Sider Lumber (Feb 2026) and CORCO (May 2026).
2026-01-15: NAHB reported an RMI reading of 64 for Q4 2025 with remodeling momentum expected to continue into 2026.
outlook: For 2026–27, the market is likely to stay in a mixed-growth regime: stable to modest growth in millwork wholesaling tied to remodeling and replacement cycles, with slower growth in pure commodity-driven new-home channels. Margin quality will depend on execution in value-added categories, freight efficiency, and the ability to offset commodity downside with service-intensive sales.
themes: Consolidation remains the primary structural theme, with acquisition-led platform expansion accelerating.
Value-added mix is becoming critical as standalone lumber/sheet-goods sensitivity to rate and housing-cycle swings increases.
Remodeling and life-cycle maintenance are acting as a partial offset to weaker new single-family momentum.
Cost control focus is shifting toward logistics, fuel, and labor productivity in branch and delivery networks.
one_sentence: NAICS 4233 millwork-related wholesalers grew slower in 2025–26 in core commodity categories, while acquisitions and service-led customization are lifting competitive positioning in remodeling and multi-family channels.

title: Millwork in the US
one_liner: A U.S. millwork market anchored in windows, doors, trim, and flooring remains resilient through remodeling demand while new construction stays soft.
overview: Millwork in the US is a construction-dependent manufacturing category supplying wood windows, doors, trim, flooring, and related architectural elements, with demand strongly tied to residential upgrades and selective commercial projects. IBISWorld baseline data places 2022 revenue at about $33.0B. Recent industry signals show remodelling has become the strongest demand pillar as affordability constraints and mortgage sensitivity keep new starts uneven.

other_2026_indicators.remodeling_spending_share: 44% of residential spending in Q1 2025 (up from 33% in 2007 context)

baseline_2022.growth: -0.95% projected CAGR from 2022 to 2028 (IBISWorld baseline); -1.27% historical CAGR 2005-2022
baseline_2022.notes: About 90% of industry products were tied to residential construction in the baseline period; nonresidential exposure was lower.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers sell through channels to home builders, remodelers, design-build contractors, distributors, and large home improvement retailers.
Revenue is project-linked: new construction windows/doors/flooring work during new builds and major renovations, plus smaller replacement and upgrade jobs.
Gross margins improve on value-added products (precision trim, custom openings, wood-facing, energy-performance features) and weaken when commodity substitutes and discount pressure intensify.
cost_structure: Material costs remain the largest swing factor: windows/doors/flooring inputs rely on lumber, engineered wood, glass, hardware, finishes, and associated packaging.
Labor is a major and rising cost due to trade and finishing skill shortages.
Energy and transport materially affect production economics; fuel-related price pressure continues through 2025-26 even as some supply-chain bottlenecks ease.
Certification, installation support, and warranty/compliance requirements add overhead in higher-performance and energy-focused product segments.
current_dynamics: Remodeling firms are increasing market share in residential construction spending, shifting demand away from purely new-build cycles.
Aging housing stock and aging-in-place retrofit demand are lifting kitchen, bath, and accessibility-adjacent upgrades.
Labor shortages remain structural, with public housing-sector indicators repeatedly citing a large number of construction openings.
Material and tariff-related uncertainty is visible in manufacturer surveys, increasing caution on inventory and lead times.
whats_growing: Remodeling-led demand (NAHB: positive trend in 2025 and forecast continuation into 2026).
Higher-value, long-tail residential upgrades such as bathroom, kitchen, and whole-house refresh projects.
Automation investments in wood/window-door facilities as manufacturers try to offset labor constraints.
Energy-performance-conscious products and premium architectural finishes in replacements and retrofits.
whats_shrinking: Single-family new-build momentum has weakened with start-rate pressure versus prior stronger periods.
Project backlogs in portions of the window and door segment were reported as softer in Q4 2025.
Price flexibility is reduced by elevated borrowing costs and labor/material inflation, limiting premium conversion for some smaller job segments.
recent_developments: 2025-02-25: NAHB reported a forecast path for remodeling growth (+5% in 2025, +3% in 2026).
2026-01-15: NAHB reported Q4 2025 Remodeling Market Index at 64, indicating sustained positive remodeler sentiment.
2026-02-18: NAHB Housing Outlook projected single-family starts at 940,000 in 2026 and 984,000 in 2027, and noted a nationwide housing deficit of 1.2 million units.
2026-02-18: NAHB indicated remodel-related housing-spending share at 44% in 2025 Q1, above 33% in 2007 benchmark context.
2026-05-05: NAHB launched quarterly State Projections of Remodeling with California at 7.9% share and $22.11B for Q4 2025 remodeling spending.
2026-05-22: NAHB said US households spent $670B on remodeling in 2024 across roughly 20M households.
outlook: The 2026-27 period is likely to be moderate but more stable than the prior new-construction-heavy cycle: growth in total industry revenue is likely constrained, while millwork tied to remodeling should hold up better than pure new-home exposure. Market participants remain focused on cost control, labor recruiting, and automation to defend margins.
themes: Remodeling-led recovery and aging-in-place demand
Substitution from wood toward composite and metal alternatives in some segments
Labor scarcity and workforce localization risk
Tariff and policy uncertainty in building materials
Automation and digitalization in manufacturing operations
Regional concentration of demand around high-value renovation markets
one_sentence: In 2025-26 the industry is moving from new-build-led growth to a remodeling-led model, with labor and material pressure still the main margin risks.

title: Mineral & Phosphate Mining in the US
one_liner: A concentrated U.S. mining segment for fertilizer minerals, industrial salts, and carbonate materials that is stabilizing through cost-control and selective demand rebounds in 2026.
overview: In 2022, IBIS sized this industry at approximately US$8.6 billion of revenue with a 9.0% profit margin and US$775 million in profit, while noting cyclical demand dependence on agriculture and industrial users. By 2024, USGS showed the wider nonfuel mineral sector at about US$106 billion in total U.S. production value, with salt and phosphate among higher-value domestic outputs. In 2025, USGS quarterly production data showed phosphate rock and soda ash rising against the same half-year in 2024, while gypsum lagged. Company-level filings in late 2025 and early 2026 indicate tighter operating control but continued sensitivity to end-user cash flow, input costs, and winter-weather swings.

notable_recent_change.value: USGS Q2 2025: phosphate production +18% QoQ; soda ash +4% QoQ

how_it_makes_money: Mine and produce marketable phosphate rock, soda ash, gypsum, and related minerals, then sell into fertilizer, chemical, glass, construction-material, and deicing markets; profitability is largely driven by throughput, realized pricing, and logistics intensity versus commodity exposure.
cost_structure: High fixed/variable mix: energy and process inputs (including sulfur, ammonia feed inputs, and processing power), transportation to downstream users, mine/site costs, and environmental/compliance spend. Cost leverage is highly volume sensitive: deicing and salt/plant-nutrition players showed meaningful profit swings from volume normalization, product mix, and per-ton cost re-absorption.
current_dynamics: US phosphate and soda ash production have shown near-term uplift in 2025 against 2024, but fertilizer demand remains highly sensitive to grower affordability and commodity cash-flow conditions. Deicing demand is still seasonal and weather-dependent; salt producers report rebound in volumes with softer blended pricing. Major trade dynamics include stronger Chinese export controls on low-analysis phosphate and uneven low-price import competition, which can lift domestic balance conditions.
whats_growing: USGS Q2 2025: phosphate rock production rose 18% versus Q1 2025.
USGS Q2 2025: soda ash production rose 4% versus Q1 2025 and 3% YTD versus 2024.
Compass Minerals reported a 20% jump in highway deicing sales volumes in FY2025 Q4 versus prior year, tied to normalization in winter demand.
Mosaic’s Jan 2026 commentary expects improving 2026 demand as growers rebuild soil nutrients after prior weak application years.
whats_shrinking: USGS Q2 2025: gypsum production declined 5% versus Q1 and -8% YTD versus 2024.
Compass reported FY2025 full-year salt pricing down 3% versus prior year, while adjusted EBITDA per ton declined versus FY2024 as it reabsorbs cost structure.
Mosaic reported Q4 2025 North American phosphate shipments down about 20% versus the prior quarter year-over-year context due weak demand and affordability pressure.
USDA long-term trend analysis shows U.S. fertilizer production, trade share, and phosphate share have weakened relative to historical baselines since 2006.
recent_developments: 2025-01-31: USGS released Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025 and reported $106 billion total U.S. nonfuel mineral production value in 2024, with salt and phosphate classified among top domestic outputs.
2026-02-04: USGS published Production of Selected Mineral Commodities in the Q2 2025 report showing phosphate and soda ash output increases while gypsum weakened.
2025-12-08: Compass Minerals reported FY2025 results with full-year deicing revenue up 13% and provided 2026 guidance of 9,650-10,300 thousand tons total salt sales.
2026-01-16: Mosaic issued market commentary and Q4 2025 sales update, noting tighter phosphate demand in late 2025 and expectation of stronger 2026 demand rebalancing.
2026-01-16: Mosaic also noted tighter supply dynamics from Chinese phosphate export controls and improved potential for higher-priced phosphate balances in 2026.
outlook: Near-term outlook is mixed but slightly constructive: production intensity appears supportive in phosphate and soda ash, while weather, fertilizer affordability, and trade policy remain the primary swing factors. Base case is modest demand recovery in agriculture and improving utilization at mineral producers, with margins improving only when volume is sustained and input-cost inflation moderates.
themes: Weather-driven deicing cyclicality
Fertilizer affordability and credit-cycle sensitivity
Trade policy effects on phosphate pricing
Cost leverage through utilization and per-ton absorption
Selective consolidation with rising operating discipline
one_sentence: The U.S. mineral and phosphate mining base remained flat-to-moderate in 2022 but is now driven by mixed 2025-2026 movements: stronger phosphate and soda ash output, unstable fertilizer demand, and weather-sensitive deicing volatility.

title: Mineral Product Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: US mineral product makers in 2026 are driven by construction demand for insulation and stone products, while facing high input costs, import competition, and uneven nonresidential spending.
overview: IBIS’ baseline still aligns with today’s picture: the industry is mature, linked to housing and broader construction demand, and sensitive to credit and energy costs. In 2026, Census data shows a strong June housing starts rebound while Census construction spending and AIA’s latest forecast both indicate that nonresidential activity is uneven, with manufacturing spending revisions sharply negative. In parallel, NAICS 327 labor and price signals show continued productivity weakness, labor-cost pressure, and high import-competition sensitivity, reinforcing continued margin discipline.

growth.ibis_growth_context: Mature 2005-2021 growth in 2021 projections remained moderate.

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is generated by selling insulation, cut stone, stucco and related nonmetallic mineral products to downstream construction, retrofitting, and industrial applications, with mineral wool and stone wool tied closely to new housing and building renovation activity; stone and mineral products also flow into broader infrastructure and industrial construction.
cost_structure: Raw materials and energy are major cost drivers, supported by transport- and freight-sensitive supply chains. Labor represents a growing fixed burden as wage and hours costs rise, while output per hour has weakened. Regulatory compliance, emissions and product-safety investments add fixed and recurring costs, and price competition from imported products remains a constant pressure point.
current_dynamics: June 2026 housing started at 1,427,000 (SAAR), with single-family starts at 895,000 (both from Census June 2026 release).
Census construction spending in June 2026 was US$2,166.5 billion, 3.2% below June 2025 levels.
BLS NAICS 327 employment rose to 423.0K in July 2026, while wages and productivity pressure widened.
BLS import and export price indexes for mineral products remain elevated, indicating price competition risk.
AIA’s July 2026 consensus lowered 2026 nonresidential growth expectation to a decline and cut manufacturing forecasts sharply.
whats_growing: Residential and renovation demand improved with higher housing activity and retrofit demand tied to comfort and energy savings.
Large-capacity and capacity modernization investments continued, notably in NA insulation manufacturing.
Demand for low-carbon, high-performance insulation is strengthened by building-efficiency policy direction.
Commercial and institutional segments tied to AI/data-center expansion and certain healthcare/amenity projects remain relatively supportive.
whats_shrinking: AIA consensus shows nonresidential manufacturing activity forecast to fall materially in 2026 versus prior stronger assumptions.
High import penetration keeps pricing disciplined and compresses margins.
Labor productivity remained weak in recent BLS NAICS 327 periods, indicating operational efficiency headwinds.
Demand in some nonresidential segments remains tied to discretionary private capex that is sensitive to financing conditions.
recent_developments: 2025-09-08: Knauf announced a major investment in Shelbyville, IN, including a new pipe-production line and expanded blowing-wool capacity (commissioning target Q2 2026).
2026-04-29: Rockwool began construction of a new Wallula, WA stone wool facility (US$175 million local investment).
2026-07-17: Census reported housing starts at 1,427,000 SAAR for June, up from June 2025.
2026-07-21: AIA lowered 2026 nonresidential construction forecast from +1.0% in January to a -0.3% to -1.4% range across panel views.
2026-08-03: Census reported June construction spending of US$2,166.5 billion, slightly below revised May.
outlook: Short term outlook remains mixed: residential-led demand should provide a floor, while nonresidential demand is expected to be uneven with stronger pockets (data centers, healthcare, institutional upgrades) and weaker manufacturing-led construction. 2027 is likely to see modest stabilization if financing and inflationary conditions improve.
themes: Housing rebound offsets uneven construction cycles
Energy-efficiency and decarbonized building demand
Persistent import-price and tariff uncertainty
Capacity modernization and automation in insulation manufacturing
Data-center and technology-enabled commercial demand as a partial offset
one_sentence: The industry remains construction-linked and mature, with housing momentum cushioning demand, but nonresidential manufacturing-led growth is still weak and inflation-adjusted unit economics are pressured.

title: Mining in the US
one_liner: US mining is split between volatile hydrocarbon extraction and slower-growth nonfuel minerals, with 2026 production still tied to oil and gas throughput while critical minerals are climbing in strategic importance.
overview: The USGS baseline for nonfuel minerals shows total U.S. nonfuel mineral production at $106 billion in 2024 and $112 billion in 2025, a 5.6% rise. Hydrocarbon-led mining remains the largest value contributor, with EIA forecasting U.S. crude output near 13.6 million b/d in 2026 and 13.8 million b/d in 2027. Coal remains operationally active but structurally weaker, while natural gas production and LNG exports are still growing on efficiency and infrastructure momentum. Labor and safety data from BLS show mining still supporting roughly 600k+ workers, with average hourly earnings near $42/worker-hour in 2026.

key_stats.market_size: n/a
key_stats.growth: n/a

baseline_2022.market_trend_note: IBIS baseline also projected sector growth to -3.72% for 2022–2028.

how_it_makes_money.hydrocarbon: Revenue is driven by crude oil and natural gas extraction, with output, quality, and price assumptions setting margins and cash flow.
how_it_makes_money.nonfuel_minerals: Revenue comes from commodity production and sales of industrial/nonfuel minerals (metals, aggregates, and chemical feedstocks) into construction, manufacturing, and technology supply chains.
how_it_makes_money.downstream_linkages: Export sales and domestic manufacturing demand convert commodity value into secondary margins via processing and processing-linked logistics.

cost_structure: Hydrocarbon drilling and completion costs are highly tied to well productivity and service-cycle pricing.
Energy inputs (fuel, power, compression, processing) are a major recurring cost in both oil-and-gas and mineral beneficiation workflows.
Labor intensity is high in extraction and operations; BLS shows ~600k+ sector workers with elevated wage levels versus the broad labor market.
Regulatory compliance, permitting, environmental review, and land-use obligations add pre-production and operating cost.
current_dynamics: Nonfuel mineral output has recovered, with USGS reporting a rise to $112 billion in 2025 from $106 billion in 2024.
EIA’s July 2026 outlook keeps U.S. crude above 13.6 million b/d and expects dry natural gas production growth to 111.25 bcf/d in 2026.
Q1 2026 coal production was 131.9 million short tons, only 0.1% below Q4 2025 and still linked to lower utility demand expectations.
BLS records 2026 mining payroll momentum (all employees about 609k, production-nonsupervisory about 457k in July 2026).
Critical mineral policy remains active, with federal efforts around permitting certainty and domestic battery-material capacity expansion.
whats_growing: Hydrocarbon-linked production volumes remain resilient in 2026 under low prices and high operating efficiency.
U.S. LNG exports increased from 15.1 bcf/d in 2025 to 17.4 bcf/d in 2026.
Demand for critical minerals in battery/clean-energy and defense-linked chains continues to pull premium-metal and processing interest.
Coal and minerals-related policy support for permitting/process capacity in frontier basins is accelerating.
whats_shrinking: Coal consumption in power generation and forecast production for 2027 is expected to decline in the EIA baseline path.
Some high-cost U.S. battery-metal segments remain pressured by import-dependent supply chain structures and price declines.
New coal mine capacity and mine counts remain under pressure even as legacy production runs down.
Profitability in parts of nonfuel extraction is still vulnerable to price shocks and volatile import competition.
recent_developments: 2025-01-31: USGS reported nonfuel mineral production rose to $106 billion in 2024 and highlighted mixed commodity performance.
2026-01-10: DOE announced up to $725 million in potential funding for domestic battery critical materials processing/manufacturing.
2026-05-15: BLM began a streamlining process for permitting in Alaska’s National Petroleum Reserve, with a 45-day scoping period.
2026-07-07: EIA’s July STEO cited U.S. crude at 13.6 million b/d in 2026 and 13.8 million b/d in 2027.
2026-07-07: EIA’s STEO framework also reported U.S. dry gas production at 111.25 bcf/d in 2026 and 115.30 bcf/d in 2027.
outlook: Near term (2026–2027), the US mining ecosystem appears split: hydrocarbon extraction remains the value anchor while coal trends remain soft, and nonfuel minerals grow where strategic demand is strongest. The main upside comes from LNG-linked gas monetization and critical-mineral industrial demand; the main downside is price-cycle sensitivity plus permitting and import-reliance risk.
themes: Energy transition raises demand for certain minerals while reducing some fossil-fuel end uses
Volatility in commodity cycles remains the primary earnings driver
Policy and permitting changes are becoming a competitive differentiator
Operational productivity and capex discipline matter more as margin expansion slows
Domestic sourcing and supply-chain resilience pressure investment into value-added processing
one_sentence: US mining remains large, cyclical, and policy-sensitive: oil and gas still dominates value, while nonfuel minerals are rising on strategic demand but remain import-reliant.

title: Mining, Oil & Gas Machinery Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: US manufacturers of mining, oil and gas machinery remain highly cyclical, balancing 2026 order recovery against unstable commodity-driven capex timing.
overview: Demand is concentrated in drill rigs, pressure-control systems, completion hardware, and replacement parts for oil and gas field operations. Operators increasingly prioritize shorter-cycle, high-efficiency equipment and reliability upgrades over broad fleet expansion, which keeps order flow uneven. This creates a recurring-cycle profile where backlog strength can improve short-term utilization, but headline spending remains sensitive to rig counts, oil prices, and capex policy.

baseline_2022.notes: 2022 baseline is derived from Census/FRED manufacturers' shipment series (U33DVS) because the provided IBIS text baseline points to 2021 values in its Jan 2022 snapshot.

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is primarily generated from sales of new drilling, completion, and field-equipment units, with meaningful recurring income from replacement parts, maintenance contracts, retrofits, software-enabled monitoring, and service-intensive installation/commissioning work. Profitability is amplified by mix shift toward high-specification, faster-payback installations and service-linked support while large legacy replacement cycles are delayed.

major_cost_drivers: Steel, forged components, and specialized alloys
Precision machining, motors, hydraulics, electronics, and controls
Freight, freight insurance, and heavy-gear logistics
Working capital and financing costs for project-based manufacturing
current_pressure_signals: 2026 BLS PPI indicates oil field and gas field machinery at +1.4% year-over-year and mining machinery and equipment at +2.6%
Inventory and labor balancing remain critical as orders arrive in lumpy batches

2026-06 rig count support remains elevated relative to spring 2026, helping field-equipment utilization.
2026-07 energy outlook still carries multi-quarter production support in the U.S., which sustains demand for replacement and reliability-focused spending.
2026-06 BLS readings for oil field and mining machinery remain positive, helping firms preserve pricing power.
whats_shrinking: 2022-to-2025 shipment totals fell from $16,275m to $15,614m.
2026-06 IP index for NAICS 33313 fell from 81.9998 in Q1 to 81.4506 in Q2, signaling uneven manufacturing momentum.
Long-cycle greenfield expansion remains constrained by oil-capex discipline and decarbonization-related uncertainty.

outlook: The industry likely trends to measured recovery in 2026 as order intake and unfilled orders rise, but demand quality remains uneven and still tied to operator capex decisions. A modestly stronger oil-cycle can lift replacement demand and utilization, while prolonged policy or inflation friction could keep spending disciplined. Winners are likely firms with broad field-service ecosystems, stronger aftermarket, and faster execution.
themes: Cycle-aware demand driven by rig counts and short-cycle upstream economics
Backlog-led production scheduling and lean plant utilization
Stronger pricing focus on reliability, safety, and automation
Industry consolidation and strategic partnerships across drilling, completions, and maintenance ecosystems
one_sentence: The industry is still demand-led by upstream drilling activity, with 2026 showing stronger order books but volatile execution as operators rebalance growth, productivity, and cash discipline.

title: Mobile Storage Services
one_liner: Mobile storage combines door-to-door container moves with short- to medium-duration storage to serve households and businesses during relocation, renovation, and temporary asset staging.
overview: IBIS-style industry definitions still describe mobile storage as a mature, low-capital services business with limited concentration and high operating competition, with demand split between residential movers and commercial users. Using 2025–2026 market signals, demand drivers are mixed: U.S. relocation activity remains supported by household moves and life changes, but high borrowing costs and volatile housing cycles are unevenly distributed by region. Existing-home transactions in 2026 remain significant (4.09 million in June, per NAR), while 2025 housing starts and single-family permits softened, moderating future relocation volume. Competitive dynamics are increasingly shaped by network coverage and service speed, with major operators expanding container networks and integrating mobile tech for pickups, storage access, and scheduling.

key_stats.market_size: USD 10.8 billion (2026 estimate derived from IBISWorld projection path from USD 10.298B in 2022 and 1.18% projected CAGR to 2028; IBISWorld noted USD 10.925B expected by 2027)
key_stats.growth: 1.18% CAGR projected (2022-2028) from IBISWorld baseline; operator-level FY2026 growth remains stronger: U-Haul moving & storage revenue increased to 5,686.69M from 5,492.77M (2026 vs 2025), +3.5% in fiscal 2026

baseline_2022.growth: 1.79% CAGR from 2005-2022; 1.18% projected CAGR from 2022-2028; projected 2027 revenue USD 10.9 billion

how_it_makes_money: Door-to-door container transport (in-town and one-way)
Short-term container storage and longer-term self-storage rentals
Ancillary rental and service fees (insurance, packing, moving supplies, logistics add-ons)
Commercial service flows (document/furniture/equipment transport and storage for business moves)
cost_structure: Fuel and trip-related transport exposure: U.S. on-highway diesel was $5.313/gal in the week ending July 27, 2026 (EIA)
Fleet intensity: U-Haul fiscal 2026 showed higher Moving and Storage costs including depreciation of rental equipment (+186.6M) and repair costs (+29.5M)
Labor and claims costs: personnel and self-insured cost increases remain major drivers in operator filings
Inventory and storage expansion capex: added ~5.3M net rentable sq ft in FY2026 (U-Haul) with additional fixed-cost burden
major_players: U-Haul (AMERCO; U-Box / broad moving and storage network)
current_dynamics: Residential relocation remains the main growth anchor; household move activity is still elevated in a cost-of-living-driven environment.
Commercial demand is stabilizing rather than collapsing as office vacancy improves (CBRE: Q2 2026 overall vacancy down 30 bps to 18.3%).
Operator scale investments continue: major networks are adding fleet and rentable capacity while pushing mobile app-based scheduling and hybrid DIY/assisted workflows.
Competitive pressure remains high as large container platforms increase geographic footprint and transparent online quoting.
whats_growing: U.S. U-Haul FY2026 showed Moving & Storage revenue growth to 5,686.7M with self-storage revenue up to 972.4M (both up year-over-year in FY2026).
Household migration narratives are strengthening toward lower-cost/high-job-growth metro clusters (PODS 2026 report).
Hybrid DIY + assisted services and at-home storage options are expanding in adoption across movers.
whats_shrinking: NAHB reported 2025 total housing starts of 1.36M, down 0.6% from 1.37M in 2024; single-family starts fell 6.9% (2025).
NAR June 2026 existing-home sales were down 2.4% month-over-month versus prior month, showing near-term softness in local residential transitions.
Net margins remain pressured by high trucking costs and elevated depreciation/claims-related costs despite demand resilience.
recent_developments: 2026-02-18: NAHB reported total U.S. housing starts for 2025 at 1.36M (down 0.6% from 2024); single-family starts fell 6.9%.
2026-06-11: NAR reported June 2026 existing-home sales at 4.09M annualized (with 4.6 months’ inventory).
2026-05-27: PODS released its sixth annual 2026 Moving Trends report and highlighted affordability-driven relocations concentrated in the Sun Belt.
2026-07-27: EIA diesel weekly table showed U.S. on-highway diesel at $5.313/gal, continuing elevated operating-cost exposure.
2026-01-27: Yardi reported Dec-2025 U.S. storage rents rose only 0.3% with a gradual-recovery view into 2026.
2026-02-27: U-Haul 2026 filing reported adding ~5.3M net rentable square feet of self-storage and 25K increase in occupied rooms on average.
outlook: Near-term outlook is likely modest and regional: sustained urban/suburban affordability stress keeps residential mobility uneven, while improving office utilization reduces the downside risk for commercial segments. Firms that combine broad container reach, mobile scheduling, and asset-light routing should outperform as consumers continue to favor flexible, low-friction moves. Base-case for 2026-27 is still positive but below high-single-digit growth; cost control in diesel, labor, and depreciation is the key value lever.
themes: relocation-as-a-service rather than one-time transport
cost sensitivity to diesel and fleet replacement cycles
network breadth as a moat in containerized moving
housing-cycle dependency via relocations and urban-to-suburban/Sun-Belt shifts
technology-enabled self-service + assisted hybrid demand
one_sentence: The U.S. mobile storage market is a modest-growth, relocation-sensitive services industry where demand is supported by housing churn and logistics scale, while margins face pressure from mobility costs and uneven regional demand.

title: Model Agencies
one_liner: US model agencies represent talent for fashion, beauty, and commerce campaigns and earn through commissions, booking fees, and licensing deals.
overview: The U.S. model agency industry earns from representing models in advertising, editorial, and commercial campaigns across apparel, beauty, entertainment, and emerging creator-activation channels. Demand remains tied to media budgets and campaign volume, but competition now includes direct social casting, creator networks, and AI-driven content workflows. Industry structure remains fragmented with a small set of legacy agencies that keep premium rosters and service depth.

key_stats.market_size: USD 3.0 billion (US, 2025)
key_stats.growth: 4.4% CAGR projected for US 2026-2033; ad-driven cycle improved with U.S. media spend +9.5% in 2026 vs 2025 (IAB)
key_stats.ad_market_link: U.S. media channels shifted fastest in social and CTV; creator/partnership formats remain high-growth

how_it_makes_money.product_licenses: remainder (~1.4%) from licensing/product collaborations and related royalty-sharing models

cost_structure.technology_and_legal: Rising spend on digital workflow tools, creator infrastructure, and AI/compliance controls (especially likeness and contract controls) increases overhead for larger agencies

2026 cyclical drivers (Olympics, World Cup, and midterms) are supporting near-term marketing budgets and campaign throughput.
Regulation and labor standards in model management (contract terms, commissions, AI-consent requirements) are adding compliance overhead and operational complexity.
Low-tier agencies face pressure from direct model-brand connects via social and creator channels that can bypass traditional booking layers.
whats_growing: 2026 media demand growth from social, creator partnerships, and CTV-linked spending.
AI-assisted talent discovery, virtual casting workflows, and digital campaign support services.
Higher compliance investment in model rights, contracts, and transparency under workforce protections.
whats_shrinking: Price-power for non-premium agencies as brands source alternatives outside traditional rosters.
Long-tail physical-only campaign models versus integrated digital-first campaign production.
Negotiation leverage for legacy commission-only workflows where brands shift toward direct creator sourcing.

outlook: 2026-2028 outlook is positive but uneven: headline ad spending should support top-line gains, while agency margins are likely to stay mixed as commoditized segments face digital disintermediation, and compliance-heavy operations rise. Premium agencies with differentiated rosters, brand relationships, and AI-enabled workflows are expected to outperform smaller operators.
themes: Ad-cycle sensitivity with rising event-driven marketing
AI augmentation without complete disintermediation
Compliance-led modernization of contract and compensation terms
Convergence of modeling and creator-ecosystem monetization
Persistent buyer concentration on quality, reach, and safety
one_sentence: In 2026, US model agencies are growing with stronger ad spend while facing AI-driven disruption, stricter model labor rules, and pressure on mid-tier margins.

title: Molybdenum & Metal Ore Mining in the US
one_liner: U.S. molybdenum mining is a volatile, commodity-driven sector where output and margins are tightly linked to steel demand, copper-byproduct economics, and trade conditions.
overview: The U.S. molybdenum and metal ore mining industry is a niche but strategic segment of mining, anchored by molybdenum as the main value driver and supplemented by associated metals mining output. Activity remains cyclical: global commodity swings, by-product dependence on copper, and exports-driven revenue swings continue to dominate performance, while 2025–2026 policy and industrial demand signals keep the forward outlook cautiously constructive rather than strongly expansionary.

title: Motion Picture & Theatrical Equipment Rental
one_liner: A US niche rental industry that supplies camera, lighting, sound, grip, and stage equipment for film, TV, commercials, and live events so producers can avoid heavy equipment ownership.
overview: The industry serves production buyers across filmed entertainment and live performance by renting short-cycle, high-value assets that are expensive to own or store in-house. In the latest public baseline coverage, US revenue is reported near the low-single-digit single-digit growth range and around roughly USD 2.4 billion in the 2022–2026 window. In 2025–2026, demand appears increasingly tied to content volume from ad-supported streaming/broadcast ecosystems and strong concert touring activity, while operators with integrated workflow support (delivery, technical staff, and remote production capability) gain an edge.

title: Motor Oil Manufacturing
one_liner: US motor oil manufacturing is a mature but resilient specialty market where demand remains tied to an aging vehicle fleet, routine maintenance, and long-haul transport despite slower EV transition headwinds.
overview: US motor oil manufacturing is centered on blending petroleum-derived and specialty additive oils used for passenger vehicles, trucks, heavy equipment, and industrial applications. In the most recent IBIS baseline update, revenue was driven largely by price pass-through from crude and by recurring replacement demand in auto parts and service channels; the IBIS outlook projects steady recovery with an estimated USD 19.5 billion revenue level by 2026 and a 3.9% annualized growth profile over the five-year horizon.

key_stats.growth: 3.9% CAGR (2021-2026 IBIS outlook)

how_it_makes_money.core_revenue: Blend and package engine and industrial oils using refined base stocks plus additive packages, then sell via auto parts stores, dealerships, quick-lube and maintenance networks, and fleet/industrial distributors.
how_it_makes_money.pricing_model: Product prices move with petroleum feedstock costs; major brands maintain premium for quality and durability positions while passing through crude-driven input changes.
how_it_makes_money.demand_anchor: Demand is repeat-purchase and mileage-driven, with stronger consumption in high-mileage and older light-vehicle segments.
how_it_makes_money.adjacent_revenue: Re-refined base-oil streams and premium synthetic formulations support margin contribution versus basic commodity oils.

cost_structure.labor_and_technical: Wage and technical staffing costs increased in 2025-2026 as firms expanded additive, formulation, and product-compliance capabilities.
cost_structure.channel_and_distribution: Retail/fleet distribution and service-channel support remain major operating cost areas.
cost_structure.sustainability_stream: Used-oil collection and re-refining investments create a circular-cost profile that improves raw-material efficiency and waste handling compliance.

current_dynamics: US transport remains heavily petroleum-driven in 2025, with motor-fuel-based applications still dominant (petroleum products accounted for about 89% of transport energy use in 2025, and gasoline (excluding ethanol) represented 52% of transport energy on an energy-content basis). Vehicle registrations remain high (about 297.5 million vehicles reported in Jan 2026), while vehicle aging continues (average light-vehicle age reached 12.8 years in 2025), sustaining maintenance cycles. At the same time, the 2025 light-duty market mix shifted: 22% of U.S. sales were hybrid/BEV/PHEV and BEV share weakened after September 2025 tax-credit expiration. Opex is increasingly shaped by both volatile crude and tighter recycling/handling requirements, while major players continue premium product launches and channel consolidation.
whats_growing: 2025-26: Older vehicle age (12.8 years in 2025) extends maintenance frequency and oil change demand.
2025-26: Used-oil recycling/re-refining activity and service channel demand remain steady, lowering net raw-material leakage.
2026 onward: Product upgrades toward higher-performance, longer-drain and EV-supporting/industrial specialty formulations in mixed-use vehicles.
whats_shrinking: 2025: Pure battery EV light-duty share weakened late in the year as U.S. tax credits for EVs expired in September.
2025-26: Short-run margin sensitivity to crude oil remained high during periods of global oversupply.

2025-12: US light-duty EV/HEV/PHEV mix reached 22%, with BEV/PHEV momentum easing after 2025 tax-credit changes.
2025-01: EIA reported Brent crude fell from about $79/bbl in Jan to about $63/bbl in Dec, signaling surplus-driven pressure in energy markets.
2026-01: EIA projected lower gasoline prices in 2026 (down 6% vs 2025) with crude share under 45% of pump price.
2026-06: EPA updated used-oil guidance, including recycling/re-refining equivalence claims (1 gallon used oil yields roughly 2.5 quarts equivalent lubricant recovery potential).
2026-03: Shell announced it retained top position in global finished lubricants for 19 consecutive years and reported a 2025 API-grade product push.
outlook: The industry is likely to remain in a moderate-growth, mature phase through 2026, with demand supported by fleet aging and maintenance intensity but constrained by slower long-term ICE decarbonization. Near-term pricing risk is still materially linked to crude and refining conditions, while longer-term competitiveness depends on execution in premium formulations, durability-led products, and circular manufacturing (used-oil reuse/re-refining).

Petroleum-input volatility and cost pass-through discipline
EV/hybrid mix causing structural shift pressure but not immediate displacement
Re-refining, sustainability compliance, and circular-lubricant models
Consolidation and differentiation in service-linked distribution

title: Motorcycle Dealership and Repair in the US
one_liner: A small-displacement shift, electrification experiments, and persistent demand softness in 2025 are reshaping a mature U.S. motorcycle dealer and repair market.
overview: The U.S. motorcycle dealership and repair industry remains mature and discretionary, with sales tied to income and confidence, and heavy dependence on new-bike retail, financing, and in-house service. Baseline IBISWorld data showed $34,421m revenue in 2022, but 2025 brought visible pullback in new-unit demand; the latest MIC-tracked 2026 Q1 data shows category-level rebound in some segments and continued structural mix shifts. Dealers are balancing vehicle sales pressure, rising product complexity (including EVs), and service economics.

overview: The U.S. motorcycle, bike and parts manufacturing ecosystem remained discretionary-driven and interest-rate sensitive in 2025, with total new motorcycle and scooter volume declining yet competitive intensity increasing in lighter-displacement, utility, and off-road-adjacent categories. In this period, riders showed stronger preference for manageable price points and lower-displacement models, while large brands used production discipline and model mix management to protect balance sheets. Parts and accessories remained critical for profitability through higher-value add-ons, replacement cycles, and accessory-led demand even as core unit sales softened.

title: Mouthwash Manufacturing
one_liner: US mouthwash manufacturing remains a mature but steady oral care segment as firms push therapeutic, preventive-value products through grocery, pharmacy, and digital channels.
overview: IBISWorld’s 2022 baseline described a mature but not collapsing US market with 2021 revenue around USD 2.546B and low long-run penetration growth, while still projecting steady upside toward 2026. Since then, newer market sources show broader oral-rinse demand strengthening, with global oral rinse estimates moving to the USD 4.30B–5.89B range and an active shift toward therapeutic positioning, natural/alcohol-free alternatives, and convenience packaging. The business remains highly brand-led, with intense competition across Colgate, Kenvue (Listerine), Procter & Gamble (Scope), Haleon, Unilever, and smaller challengers, making margin performance highly sensitive to advertising, retail execution, and shopper acquisition.

title: Movie & Video Distribution in the US
one_liner: US movie-and-video distribution is shifting from theater/physical channels toward streaming-first, with theatrical rebounds still below pre-pandemic levels.
overview: US movie and video distribution remains a volatile intermediary layer between studios, broadcasters, exhibitors, and consumers. In 2022 the baseline IBIS profile showed a decline trend, but 2025–2026 data shows the market rebalancing: theaters remain relevant for high-value theatrical releases while consumer attention and spend increasingly move to streaming subscriptions and digital home-entertainment formats.
how_it_makes_money: Distributors and exhibitors earn from rights licensing across theatrical, TV/linear, VOD, EST, and home-entertainment windows; transaction fees from transactional video-on-demand and subscriptions; and increasingly from bundled deals and platform licensing to global streaming operators.
cost_structure: Digitization has lowered replication, storage, and physical logistics costs, but rights clearances, marketing, release window management, and premium content acquisition/creation costs remain high. Distributors are scaling toward lower fixed physical costs and higher variable content/rights and platform economics.
current_dynamics: 2019–2025 theatrical benchmark remains a drag on distributor volumes: North American industry box office in 2025 was about $8.9B versus $11.4B pre-pandemic. Home entertainment is increasingly subscription-led, with home video transactions weakened relative to streaming. Nielsen TV-viewing data shows streaming overtaking broadcast+cable in 2025 and reaching close to 50% share by mid-2026 in ad-supported categories, reinforcing pullaway from legacy linear windows.
whats_growing: 2025 subscription streaming spending reached 57.5B USD in full-year U.S. home entertainment.

Premium hybrid and AVOD/FAST models gained share inside streaming households.
4K UHD and prestige theatrical-to-digital chains supported faster monetization for select new releases.
whats_shrinking: Traditional retail/physical home-entertainment channels declined through 2025 and 2026.
Theater-based box-office share of overall audience monetization weakened versus total viewing time on screens.
Standalone VOD and transaction-only channels remained under pressure versus bundled subscriptions.
Small independent distribution margins were compressed by studios’ direct-to-consumer and direct licensing capabilities.

2026-06-23: Nielsen reported streaming captured 46.6% of ad-supported TV in Q1 2026 while ad-supported TV remained about 73% of total.
outlook: The distribution value chain is expected to continue shrinking in legacy channels while growing in platform-mediated, digitally delivered channels. Near-term growth is likely in library monetization, window re-packaging, and ad-backed streaming inventory, while independent theatrical windows remain vulnerable to blockbuster cadence and release strategy shifts by studios.
