title: Movie & Video Production in the US
one_liner: US movie and video production remains concentrated, IP-led, and increasingly financed around theatrical-plus-streaming monetization, while attendance quality trends are improving as volume remains uneven.
overview: The industry is still anchored by large studio ecosystems, but output is more selective and portfolio-driven than during peak years. 2025 showed a modest domestic theatrical rebound, while 2026 remained volatile on a year-to-date basis. Employment and attendance remained mixed: box-office-related jobs and exhibit traffic improved in some windows, but production volume and headcount trends still reflect the post-strike, post-pandemic normalization path rather than full recovery.

growth.motion_picture_exhibition_and_production: decline (2016 Feb: 234.0k, 2026 Feb: 185.2k; 10-year drop indicated as part of industry chart)

baseline_2022.additional: Projected growth in IBIS outline for 2021–2027 was +2.29% CAGR

how_it_makes_money: Theatrical box office via U.S./global release windows.
Domestic and international licensing, broadcast, and streaming/AVOD/SVOD rights after theatrical windows.
Ancillary monetization including international distribution, merchandising, and branded formats.
Exhibitor economics for the industry chain (admissions share, concessions, ticket fees, advertising).
cost_structure: High front-loaded production + post-production + talent/crew costs make portfolio selection and franchise concentration central to margins.
Marketing and release-window spend remain structurally material and competitive among major studio slates.
Exhibition-side economics are heavily influenced by film rental/share economics, with AMC reporting film exhibition costs of 48.1% of admissions revenue in 2025.
Labor intensity remains high: MPA reports high average direct wage levels in film/TV distribution and production channels.
current_dynamics: 2025 US box office reached USD 8.656B (+1.0% vs 2024), but 2026 was weaker on an annualized run basis at USD 5.655B.
The BLS CES-based monthly workforce profile shows production-exhibition exposure and strikes still suppressing momentum into 2026.
MPA’s 2024 update shows the broader film/TV ecosystem at 2.01M jobs and USD 202B wages, indicating the sector is still wage-intensive and broad-based.
AMC’s 2025 filing shows admissions revenue improved (+3.6%) while attendance fell (-2.1%), implying a pricing-led attendance mix shift.
whats_growing: Ticket and per-patron yields remain stronger than attendance volume in several exhibitor-led revenue channels.
International and franchise-linked slate monetization remains the preferred risk-adjustment strategy.
2025 Q2–Q4 NAICS 5121 activity and exhibitor results indicate resilience among high-performing titles despite aggregate volatility.
whats_shrinking: Theatrical volume share in 2026 year-to-date remains weaker than 2025 levels on an annualized basis.
BEA-reported PCE admissions spending fell from USD 11.623B (2024) to USD 10.680B (2025), signaling weaker household theater spend.
BLS indicates motion picture production employment is below its post-2022 peak and remains below pre-2022/late-2022 highs.
recent_developments: 2025-12-31: AMC (2025 Form 10-K): total revenues up 4.6%, admissions revenues up 3.6% with attendance down 2.1% (224.2m to 219.4m patrons).
2026-02-10: MPA film & TV release update: 2.01M jobs, USD 202B wages, over 162,000 businesses.
2026-02-26: Warner Bros. Discovery Q4 2025 shareholder letter: $4.4B 2025 global box office for Studios and 2026 slate acceleration guidance.
2026-06-03: FRED updated NAICS 5121 employment at 413.9k (2025 annual).
2026-08-07: BLS industry profile updated with latest subsector workforce and establishment data for NAICS 5121.
outlook: The near term appears to favor selective output from proven IP, globalized licensing, and stronger margin discipline over broad volume growth; production firms that can pair theatrical hooks with direct streaming economics are better positioned than those relying on theatrical volume alone.
themes: Concentration: a limited studio set drives most global theatrical and franchise upside.
Pricing-led recovery: premium formats, higher ticketing, and yield management are carrying exhibitor economics while volumes remain inconsistent.
Portfolio reset: studios are balancing tentpoles with lower-capex content formats for platform-first monetization.
one_sentence: In 2025–2026, theatrical demand stabilized versus 2024 and production/exhibition economics became more concentrated in major studios, with cost discipline and platform expansion offsetting weaker volume and high volatility in release quality.

title: Movie Rental Kiosks
one_liner: The U.S. movie rental kiosk model is in terminal decline as streaming and ad-supported digital formats continue to outgrow physical media.
overview: The movie rental kiosk industry remains structurally tied to physical DVDs, Blu-rays, and games, but long-term demand is being replaced by streaming-led home entertainment spending. Baseline IBIS reporting already showed revenue contraction through 2021 and projected a slow decline into 2026, and 2025–2026 market data now shows physical media spending falling while subscription-driven digital consumption reaches record scale. In 2024–2025 Redbox, the category leader, became a balance-sheet and bankruptcy-related risk point after the parent company entered restructuring, reinforcing that the business is not recovering despite ongoing efforts in digital add-on services.

key_stats.market_size: U.S. physical home-entertainment formats (DVD/Blu-ray/4K UHD) spent $870.0 million in 2025 (DEG physical product category, 2025)
key_stats.growth: Physical formats declined 9.3% in 2025 versus 2024; subscription streaming rose 19.8% in 2025 to $57.5 billion (92%+ of total home entertainment spend)
key_stats.2021_ibis_reference: IBIS-style 2021 baseline for the industry shows ~$705.0 million market size with weak margins and declining kiosks
key_stats.kiosk_presence: CSSE bankruptcy filing in 2024 references Redbox’s kiosk network at approximately 27,000 units

baseline_2022.market_size: ~$681 million (IBIS-style estimate for 2022, derived from 2021 decline pattern and 2021 baseline trend)

how_it_makes_money: Rental and sale transactions at automated kiosks for DVDs/Blu-rays and games (legacy Redbox model).
Premium media mix: higher-priced Blu-ray and premium rentals previously used to defend margins.
Digital TVOD/EST transactions through branded on-demand channels.
Ancillary kiosk-related revenue from merchandizing, installation, and advertising at kiosk touchpoints.
cost_structure: Content licensing and studio-release relationships (especially new-release windows and inventory refresh rights) remain a core pass-through/availability cost driver.
Physical network operating cost is high: kiosk footprint, replenishment logistics, and field maintenance/compliance (2021 IBIS classifies the industry as high-capital intensity).
Location economics matter: commission/placement economics and site-level performance drive unit-level profitability.
Debt and restructuring overhead became material for the dominant player during 2024 Chapter 11/7 transition events.
major_players: Redbox (largest legacy kiosk operator; roughly 32,000 kiosks in 2022 disclosures, ~27,000 in 2024 filing)
Netflix (major streaming substitute; 72% of surveyed U.S. adults used in Apr 2025)
Amazon Prime Video (67% of surveyed U.S. adults used in Apr 2025)
Disney+ (48% of surveyed U.S. adults used in Apr 2025)
Hulu (52% of surveyed U.S. adults used in Apr 2025)
Max (formerly HBO Max), Paramount+, Peacock, Apple TV+ (competing streaming set in 2025 usage data)
current_dynamics: Streaming services remain dominant in household consumption; Pew 2025 shows 83% of U.S. adults use streaming.
Physical formats still decline in aggregate but show some cushioning from premium 4K UHD segments in 2025.
Category has moved from multi-operator competition to effectively single-player dominated legacy operations with financial stress-driven shrinkage.
whats_growing: Streaming monetization: 2025 DEG data shows streaming (SVOD + hybrid) up 19.8% for 2025, to $57.5 billion.
Hybrid ad-supported streaming tier activity accelerated in 2025 and remained a meaningful share driver within streaming mix.
Kiosk incumbents are expanding digital layers (TVOD/FAST/AVOD) to monetize installed-brand awareness outside kiosk-only transactions.
whats_shrinking: Physical home-entertainment product spending fell 23.4% in 2025’s 2024 baseline year (from 2023 to 2024) and then 9.3% in 2025.
DEG reports kiosk-dominant physical rental channels losing traffic to digital convenience and larger streaming windows.
Redbox kiosk ecosystem contracted from around 32,000 units in 2022 disclosures to ~27,000 units reported in 2024 filings.
Digital transaction spending is volatile and increasingly tied to release quality; Q4 2025 saw weaker transactional uplift while major budget categories continued to tilt toward subscriptions.
recent_developments: 2024-06-28: Chicken Soup for the Soul filing disclosed Redbox’s business context with ~27,000 kiosks and stressed financial leverage (about $970 million debt in filing exhibits).
2024-07-10: U.S. Bankruptcy Court issued Order converting CSSE cases from Chapter 11 to Chapter 7.
2025-02-14: DEG Year-End 2024 report showed U.S. home-entertainment spend near $57.2 billion and physical formats down 23.4% to $959.6 million.
2025-07-01: Pew (Apr 2025 survey window) reported 83% of U.S. adults used streaming services.
2026-02-11: DEG Year-End 2025 report showed physical formats at $870.0 million, down 9.3% YoY, while subscription streaming reached $57.5 billion (19.8% growth).
outlook: For 2026, the kiosk channel is likely to remain a shrinking legacy channel with further location rationalization and selective survival only where kiosk economics remain positive (high-traffic, low-touch convenience locations plus premium-title availability). Industry outcome is less a rebound and more managed attrition toward digital-first home entertainment and niche physical media demand (collectable/collector-focused formats).
themes: Substitution to streaming is no longer a trend; it is the structural baseline.
Physical formats are not dead in all forms but are moving to premium catalog and collector demand.
Legacy hardware businesses face liquidation or deep shrink cycles when parent balance sheets weaken.
Kiosk convenience is insufficient against 24/7 app-based and subscription alternatives.
Scale consolidation has effectively reduced competitive friction among physical operators.
one_sentence: By 2026 the kiosk model has shifted from a national convenience channel to a shrinking legacy platform, with physical media demand weakening even as streaming ecosystems expand.

title: Moving Services in the US
one_liner: U.S. household and commercial relocation activity is rebounding around high-house-prices, with a moderately growing moving and storage market led by route-heavy, technology-backed operators.
overview: IBISWorld’s 2026 U.S. Moving Services analysis places the market at $25.7 billion in 2026, with 9,430 operating businesses and moderate multi-year growth. Demand is increasingly concentrated in high-mobility corridors, especially into Sun Belt markets, while operators balance margin pressure from labor and fuel with route expansion and higher-value service bundles.

key_stats.competition_note: competition level described as low and decreasing

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes from moving jobs that combine transport, loading/unloading labor, packing support, and optional add-ons.
Residential relocations and cross-country/interstate moves are the largest core revenue segment.
Commercial relocation and office move projects add higher-value contracts but can be cyclical.
Storage and long-duration rentals generate recurring revenue outside the move date.
Software-enabled margins depend on job-level pricing, dispatch efficiency, and ancillary service attachment.
cost_structure: Labor is the dominant variable cost because moving remains physically intensive and service quality is labor-driven.
Fuel/diesel is a key volatile input for trucking-heavy and long-haul operators.
Fleet expansion to match destination corridors raises fixed-cost pressure in trucks, trailers, and maintenance.
Warehousing and storage costs rise with peak seasonal inventory handling and longer lead times.
SmartMoving’s 2026 benchmark work highlights that firms with stronger KPI tooling and standardized sales/dispatch execution sustain higher margin outcomes.
current_dynamics: IBISWorld’s May 2026 release shows the U.S. market at $25.7bn, up with steady long-cycle expansion.
The same release notes a shift in service geography toward Sun Belt destination demand corridors.
Census 2026 data show 1,358,700 housing units started in 2025 and 1,404,000 SAAR privately-owned starts in Dec 2025.
NAR data indicate June 2026 existing-home sales at 4.09 million SAAR (+2.8% year-over-year) with a 4.6-month inventory balance.
Transport-sector labor in May 2026 was 6,597,500 employed (seasonally adjusted), with warehousing and storage above 1.8 million in the same sector profile.
whats_growing: Sun Belt destination demand and repeat-route routing intensity are strengthening.
Industry tools and KPI-driven operations are expanding, especially among larger regional operators.
Demand for packing, storage, and storage-plus-move bundles is increasingly bundled in one-sales workflow.
Commercial relocation activity is stabilizing as firms resume growth plans.
whats_shrinking: Volume sensitivity remains high when housing affordability weakens.
Margin dispersion is widening between operationally disciplined firms and fragmented operators.
Smaller operators face higher financing, payroll, and fleet-utilization risk as route distances increase.
Labor and fuel volatility continue to squeeze underpriced operators.
recent_developments: 2026-02-26: SmartMoving announced a 2026 State of Moving Report webinar highlighting margin dispersion and KPI standards from 484 participating movers.
2026-05-27: SmartMoving published findings from its 2026 State of Moving Report survey of hundreds of movers.
2026-05-27: PODS released its sixth annual Moving Trends Report; affordability was cited as a top relocation motivator.
2026-05-27: U-Haul reported FY2026 results, with moving and storage EBITDA improving and self-moving rental revenues up 2.3% year-over-year.
2026-07-09: NAR reported June 2026 existing-home sales of 4.09 million SAAR (+2.8% year-over-year), median existing-home price $440,600.
2026-07-23: Freddie Mac PMMS showed the U.S. 30-year fixed-rate mortgage at 6.58%.
outlook: The near-term outlook is for continued but still moderate growth as migration and relocation remain above historical lows, while profitability is expected to separate operators by operational discipline.
themes: Housing-cycle sensitivity
Sun Belt migration concentration
Labor and fuel cost pressure
Fleet and route-network optimization
Data-driven dispatch and pricing
Consolidation toward higher-discipline operators
one_sentence: The industry in 2026 remains labor-heavy and margin-sensitive, with growth tied to housing turnover, regional migration corridors, and operational discipline.

title: Musical Groups & Artists in the US
one_liner: U.S. musicians are shifting most of their earnings from recorded music sales to live touring plus streaming royalties, with 2025 showing a major recovery in recorded-revenue scale but mixed momentum on live ticket economics.
overview: The 2022 IBIS baseline captured a post-pandemic recovery phase after the 2020 collapse, while 2025-2026 data shows a stronger streaming economy and still-thriving global touring activity. The market is now dominated by subscription streaming and premium fan access, with live events acting as a critical profitability engine but with signs of demand normalization after extreme rebound years.

key_stats.market_size: $11.5B US wholesale recorded music revenue in 2025 (RIAA)

baseline_2022.market_size: $5.894B industry revenue (2021 baseline shown in 2022 report)

how_it_makes_money.description: Live touring, festivals, and venue appearances remain a core high-value channel. In the older IBIS filing, live performance represented 31.6% of revenue and is structurally favored because it is harder to substitute digitally.
The largest and fastest-growing income stream in 2025, with premium paid subscriptions now the biggest contributor of US music revenue.
how_it_makes_money.trend: Dominant: 52.4% of global streaming share remained high in 2025 and paid subscriptions exceeded half of US total revenue.

how_it_makes_money.description: Downloads and much traditional digital unit consumption continue to decline in unit and revenue terms, while vinyl is rebounding.
how_it_makes_money.trend: US physical includes a mix of slower CDs and strong vinyl growth.

how_it_makes_money.description: License payments for placements, public performance, and publishing remains a meaningful but cyclical income source.
how_it_makes_money.trend: US sync was flat-to-soft in 2025 in RIAA reported split.

how_it_makes_money.description: Artists increasingly package touring and creator communities with direct fan products and bundles.
how_it_makes_money.trend: Higher direct-to-fan share as artist toolkits and social-commerce improve.

cost_structure: Tour production and payroll (crew, technicians, security, logistics, travel)
Venue guarantees, ticketing fees, insurance, and promoter/agent commissions
Content creation expenses (recording, editing, design, mastering, video)
Marketing and fan-acquisition spend (social distribution, PR, advertising)
Royalties, legal administration, and rights-clearing/licensing compliance
current_dynamics: Streaming-led economics deepened in 2025, with premium audio subscriptions becoming the largest value pillar in US music revenue.
Touring remains large in scale with lower-growth conditions than peak rebound years, especially on average ticket price and per-show volume mix.
Physical music format demand is bifurcated: vinyl and collectible formats hold, while downloads and some digital legacy segments decline.
Rights and royalty policy is again a competitive differentiator as digital performance rates and licensing transparency remain contested.
whats_growing: US premium paid subscriptions reached 106.5M in 2025 and drove 55.3% share of total US recorded revenue.
US total recorded music revenue rose 9.3% in 2025 to $11.5B wholesale.
US streaming revenue rose 3.1% in 2025 to $9.4745B.
Global recorded music reached $31.7B in 2025 with +6.4% growth.
US touring structure shows higher per-venue averages at stadium scale (average stadium gross +19% in 2025).
whats_shrinking: US non-premium digital subscriptions fell by 4.5%; free streaming was flat-to-down.
US download revenue continued to drift lower in 2025.
US synchronization income in 2025 declined year-over-year in the RIAA table (-1.3%).
Worldwide Top 100 touring gross dropped 6.1% in 2025 versus 2024.
Global ticket numbers for 2025 were 3.7% lower than 2024 despite high absolute scale.
recent_developments: 2025-09-09: RIAA released a US 2025 mid-year report showing 2025 momentum continuing into the year with over 5.0M+ total paid subscription accounts and strengthening total revenue against 2024.
2026-03-16: RIAA reported US wholesale recorded-music revenue at a record $11.5B in 2025.
2026-03-16: RIAA reported 106.5M paid subscriptions in the US, with $5.8811B premium paid subscription revenue.
2026-03-18: IFPI Global Music Report 2026 showed global recorded music up 6.4% to $31.7B in 2025 and highlighted streaming fraud and AI policy as major industry issues.
2025-12-23: Pollstar reported 2025 worldwide top-100 touring gross at $8.9B, down 6.1% from 2024, with 67.3M tickets.
outlook: Near-term growth is expected to stay robust for recorded-streaming distribution and artist-centric direct commercialization, while touring margins may remain uneven as post-rebound normalization continues. The sector should benefit from continued royalty modernization and platform investment in rights infrastructure, but policy noise around streaming accounting and synthetic activity could pressure creator economics.
themes: Streaming dominance
Live-event normalization after recovery
Direct-to-fan monetization
AI and anti-fraud governance in music distribution
Royalty and licensing standardization
Vinyl-led physical premiumization
one_sentence: US recorded music reached a new wholesale high of $11.5B in 2025 while global touring remains large but stabilized after a 2025 pullback in gross growth.

title: Musical Instrument & Supplies Stores in the US
one_liner: The U.S. music instrument retail market is recovering from a 2024 slowdown, with large chains and marketplaces using experience-led services, AI-assisted selling, and off-price channels to defend share.
overview: In 2025-2026, U.S. musical-instrument-store-related activity (NAICS 4511 proxy) shows re-acceleration in output versus 2024, supported by stronger in-store engagement and national retailer-led digital initiatives, while independent operators face margin and competitive pressure from large-format and marketplace channels.

revenue_streams: 2025-2026: instrument, accessory, and software/electronic gear sales
Repair, tuning, rentals, and music lessons
Premium service and education-led upsells tied to in-store traffic
Close-out and open-box off-price channels (including dedicated online formats)

major_costs: Merchandise and inventory costs under competitive imported-good pressure
Store rent/occupancy and workforce costs (including commissions and sales staff time)
Marketing and digital/omnichannel spend to protect traffic versus marketplaces
Markdown and clearance cost to move slow-moving stock

margin_context.unit_labor_cost_signal: Unit labor costs index 100.439 in 2025; down from 110.405 in 2024

major_players: Guitar Center (more than 300 stores and large lessons/repair/rental ecosystem; 2026)
Musician’s Friend (repositioned as premium off-price outlet, 2026)
Sweetwater (claiming largest direct-selling position in pro music gear in the U.S., 2025)
Walmart Marketplace (launched Premium Musical Instrument Shop, 2026)
current_dynamics: Demand is stabilizing but structurally bifurcated: core chains are betting on service and in-store relevance (including AI shopping aids and media content), while broad music-category sales remain exposed to powerful e-commerce channels and marketplace competition.
whats_growing: 2025-2026: in-store experience investment and music education content as a retention driver
2026: off-price premium inventory formats within large chains to convert excess/open-box stock
2025: digital assistance tools (AI in-store advisor) to improve shopping conversion
2026: marketplace-format premium music assortments expanding at national platforms
whats_shrinking: 2024: independent specialist footprint contraction (Sam Ash closed all stores; 42 locations)
Margin expansion for stand-alone physical retailers remains limited under discount and comparison-shopping pressure
2024->2025 legacy mixed-category recovery was uneven versus 2021-2024 volatility
recent_developments: 2024-05-02: Sam Ash announced all U.S. store locations would begin closing sales, effectively shuttering its remaining footprint.
2025-01-22: Guitar Center reported 6.6% preliminary holiday sales growth and said customers spent 20% more time in-store in Q4.
2025-07-21: Guitar Center launched a nationwide in-store AI shopping assistant (Rig Advisor) for live gear recommendations.
2026-01-20: Walmart launched a Premium Musical Instrument Shop on Walmart Marketplace.
2026-05-04: Guitar Center relaunched Musician’s Friend as a dedicated off-price online outlet with discounts up to 45%.
outlook: 2026 outlook is cautiously positive at the sector level, with low-to-mid single-digit output recovery likely if discretionary spending stays firm, but with further consolidation and continued pressure on independent operators unless they differentiate through service depth, education, and local inventory execution.
themes: Omnichannel migration to blended in-store + online service models
Experiential retail replacing pure transactional instrument sales
Consolidation and repositioning of inventory through off-price channels
Marketplace expansion by mega-retailers into premium music categories
AI-enabled sales guidance and customer education as competitive tools

title: National Parks & Other Nature Institutions
one_liner: The U.S. national parks and related nature institutions remain a high-demand, low-volume-cost-growth sector in 2026, with pricing reforms and constrained public budgets driving new operating pressure.
overview: This sector is led by federal and partner-operated nature institutions focused on outdoor access, conservation, interpretation, and visitor experience. Operators historically rely on admissions, concessions, and philanthropy; many remain highly public-sector dependent with persistent deferred-maintenance needs. In 2025 the National Park System logged 323,014,305 recreation visits, while 2026 policy changes shifted fee collection mechanics through residency-based pass tiers and per-person surcharges in top-traffic parks.

how_it_makes_money: Admissions and pass fees (including vehicle/visitor and park-specific fee collection)
Concessions (lodging, food, retail, tours, transportation, parking)
Donations and grants via partners and philanthropy channels
Commercial service agreements and concession franchise structures
Recurring annual pass products and timed/ancillary visit products

major_cost_drivers: Facility operations and deferred maintenance obligations
Climate-weather disruption management (closures, fire/snow response, seasonal re-planning)

current_dynamics: Post-2025 recovery remains demand-strong but visitor expansion is flatter than 2024 peak levels.
Fee architecture changed in 2026 with residency-based annual passes and nonresident surcharge logic in top parks.
Federal operational budget tables show ONPS budget authority reduced from 2026 enacted to 2027 request, increasing pressure on staffing and maintenance prioritization.
Private and local partners are increasingly important for service quality where core public budgets lag.
whats_growing: Use of digital fee and pass systems for faster entry and better fee enforcement.
Concentration of on-site spending toward lodgings and transport-linked visitor behavior (high value-per-trip segments).
Partnership and private support channels, especially for upgrades and programmatic enhancements.
whats_shrinking: 2025 visitation remained below the 2024 record (-2.7% YoY).
Per-park funding flexibility under ONPS 2027 request appears tighter versus FY2026 enacted profile.
Free-access attractiveness for nonresidents narrowed through fee-tier policy changes.

2026-01-01: Free-entrance days in 2026 designated for U.S. citizens and residents, with nonresidents generally paying entrance and surcharge charges.
2026-03-13: NPS reported 323,014,305 recreation visits and 1,386,749,187 visitor-hours in calendar year 2025; 26 parks set records.

outlook: Short-term outlook for 2026-27 is stable but more price-sensitive: visitor volumes remain high and diversified across top destinations, yet fiscal pressure increases the need for fee compliance and concession optimization. Mid-term industry structure likely shifts toward tighter operating prioritization, digital channel monetization, and selective expansion where environmental capacity and yield support higher service quality.
themes: visitor demand resilience with demand-management pressure
residency-based pricing and access policy
digital pass infrastructure
public-private conservation partnerships
maintenance backlog and deferred-capital triage
low automation, high labor sensitivity
one_sentence: Demand is robust around flagship nature destinations, but fee restructuring and tighter federal operations budgets are forcing operators toward stronger monetization, partnerships, and service prioritization.

title: Natural Disaster & Emergency Relief Services in the US
one_liner: A mission-critical, demand-driven sector of nonprofit-led service providers supported by private donations and federal disaster aid.
overview: The market is small but essential and highly exposed to weather and climate shocks. The largest service providers are nonprofit operators and community partners, while FEMA and other federal agencies coordinate and fund major declared-disaster response and recovery programs. 2022 was a volatile year in the IBIS baseline, but demand remained elevated into 2025–2026 as severe fire, flood, wind, and tornado activity increased.

key_stats.market_size: US$14.9 billion (2026E, implied from US$14.122 billion in 2022 and 1.3% CAGR trajectory)
key_stats.growth: 1.3% annualized (2022-2028 IBIS trajectory)
key_stats.disaster_frequency: 23 U.S. billion-dollar weather/climate disasters in 2025 (US$115.0 billion damages, 276 fatalities)
key_stats.workforce_shock: FEMA active employees fell by 2,446 between 2025-01-01 and 2025-06-01

how_it_makes_money.primary: Donations from households, households-plus-corporate giving, and grants/partnerships are the largest revenue stream.
how_it_makes_money.government_funding: Federal and state/local public emergency relief funding through FEMA-led declared-disaster mechanisms, including public assistance and aid programs.
how_it_makes_money.other: In-kind donations, corporate sponsorship, philanthropy-led emergency campaigns, and emergency response service contracts.

cost_structure: Labor-intensive field operations, case management, shelter logistics, and recovery coordination.
Volunteer management, transportation, warehousing, emergency warehousing, and short-cycle procurement.
High administrative and reporting overhead during declaration, aid application, and compliance cycles.
major_players: National Voluntary Organizations Active in Disaster (NVOAD)
State and local emergency management agencies
current_dynamics: Demand is still driven by clustering severe disasters; 2025 included major wildfire, flooding, and severe-weather shocks with nationwide relief activity.
Federal program capacity is constrained by workforce shrinkage, while open disaster caseloads remain elevated.
Private relief activity is still growing, but service quality is increasingly sensitive to grant timing, staffing, and coordination capacity.
whats_growing: 2025-2026 demand for emergency shelter, food support, household aid, and disaster recovery coordination due to high-loss events.
Formal coordination infrastructure is expanding (e.g., national long-term recovery mapping and VOAD coordination activity in 2025).
Federal discretionary disaster funding levels are rising (FY2026 DRF request above FY2025.
whats_shrinking: FEMA deployable workforce availability is under pressure, with significant attrition through 2025 and workforce reduction programs.
Operational flexibility declines during concurrent events when open federal support cases remain high.
Margins are not a strategic objective; non-profit financial slack is constrained while service demand spikes.

2025-06-30: American Red Cross FY25 period reported >117,000 households given direct assistance and 5.1M+ meals/snacks, with FY25 disaster relief expenses of US$625.4 million.
2025-09-02: GAO report found FEMA active employees dropped from 25,800 to 23,350 between 2025-01-01 and 2025-06-01, including 2,446 reductions.
2025-09-17: GAO follow-up reported staffing pressure in concurrent emergencies and stated only 12% of FEMA incident-management workforce was available at start of 2025 season periods.
2026-03-09: Climate Central reported 2025 had 23 U.S. billion-dollar disasters with US$115.0 billion total direct cost.
2026-09-30: NVOAD launched a nationwide long-term recovery mapping initiative for Long-Term Recovery Group coordination.
outlook: Near-term growth is likely to remain event-driven with modest trend growth but elevated volatility. If climate-related hazard frequency remains high, operating demand should stay above trend while margin pressure continues unless federal staffing and deployment capacity and private donation channels both improve.
themes: Climate volatility and severe-weather concentration
Public-private relief interdependence
Capacity strain in surge response
Local coordination and volunteer management
Long-term recovery and housing/household stabilization
Data-led triage and disaster mapping
one_sentence: Natural disaster and emergency relief in the US is growing modestly overall but remains highly volatile because demand is event-driven and funding quality is tied to disaster intensity.

title: Natural Food Coloring Manufacturing
one_liner: US natural food coloring makers are gaining scale as clean-label reformulation accelerates under the 2025–2026 federal synthetic-dye transition.
overview: Natural food coloring manufacturing produces plant- and mineral-derived color ingredients used in beverages, dairy, bakery, snacks, confectionery, and prepared foods, with growth tied to consumer preference for transparent cleaner-label formulations and faster regulatory pressure on synthetic pigments.

key_stats.market_size: US natural food color market size was USD 563.0 million in 2025 and USD 602.5 million estimated for 2026 (Grand View Research, US Horizon outlook); global natural food colors were USD 2.3 billion in 2025 and USD 2.5 billion in 2026 (Grand View Research).
key_stats.growth: US natural food color market CAGR is 7.1% for 2026–2033 (Grand View Research); US natural segment in food colors has a 6.2% CAGR in food colors overall 2025–2033; 2025 to 2026 US natural color growth is about 7.0%.
key_stats.other: US food colors market total was USD 734.4 million in 2024 and USD 1,230.2 million projected by 2033, showing faster long-run scale than the older 2020 IBIS series baseline.

baseline_2022.market_size: USD 271.1 million (estimated from IBISWorld 2020 USD 254.1 million and the 2020–2025 annualized trajectory of ~3.29%, then applied to 2022).
baseline_2022.source_note: 2019–2025 IBISWorld baseline values and forecasts are the historical anchor; 2022 value is derived from the IBIS 2020 base and 2020–2025 trend.

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is earned from B2B ingredient sales to food and beverage processors, usually via ingredient contracts, application support, and volume-based conversion programs for reformulated products where customers shift from synthetic to natural color systems.
cost_structure: Key cost drivers are agricultural/raw ingredient sourcing, extraction and stabilization process complexity, stringent food-safety compliance and filing costs, and increasing R&D for color stability across temperature/pH/light profiles; pricing is pressured when higher production and raw-cost volatility outweigh premium clean-label pricing.
major_players: Givaudan Sense Colour (former DDW, The Color House)
current_dynamics: Rapid migration planning from synthetic to natural colors accelerated after the April 22, 2025 federal phase-out announcements.
US processors are signing and executing timelines, especially in school channels and branded cereals/snacks.
New natural color approvals in 2025 improved formulators' options for bright blue and broader shade matching.
Supply-chain concentration is increasing as leading players expand US manufacturing and logistics footprints.
Volatility persists in agricultural input prices and logistics, creating margin headwinds versus formula flexibility gains.
whats_growing: Consumer health/clean-label pressure in 2025–2026 driving sustained conversion.
Public pledges by brands to remove certified synthetic dyes in 2026 and by 2027, raising demand certainty.
Natural blue and berry/purple hues from newer sources, where performance improvements are in active development.
US manufacturing capacity additions and innovation investment by category leaders.
Downstream demand from beverages, dairy, frozen desserts, and snack reformulations.
whats_shrinking: Sales dependence on certified petroleum-based food colors in mass products, especially in categories with clear public commitments to remove dyes by 2026–2027.
Use of older synthetic palettes where brand reformulation timelines are now explicit.
Small-formula innovation without supply-chain scale, as larger integrated players capture reformulation programs.
recent_developments: 2025-04-22: HHS/FDA announced a national standard and timeline to phase out six petroleum-based synthetic dyes by end of 2026 and remove remaining obsolete dye authorizations.
2025-05-09: FDA approved three natural food color petitions (Galdieria extract blue, butterfly pea extract, calcium phosphate) and expanded approved use cases.
2025-12-12: FDA tracker listed multiple major CPG pledges to complete synthetic-color removal in schools and full retail portfolios through 2026–2027.
2025-06-10: Oterra opened a 155,000 sq ft U.S. innovation/manufacturing logistics hub in Mt. Pleasant, WI to support conversion demand.
2026-01-14: Oterra reported 2024/25 revenue up 7.2% to EUR 447.1 million and EBITDA up 37.9%.
2026-08-24: FDA set final comment deadline on proposed Citrus Red No. 2 revocation.
outlook: Baseline 2025–2026 data suggest steady expansion, with the U.S. natural color market forecast to continue above 7% annual growth over the current decade and policy-driven reformulations likely to keep 2026–2027 as a transition inflection period; 2026 industry demand is expected to broaden beyond beverages into more snack, cereal, and ambient categories.
themes: Regulatory acceleration (dye phase-out deadlines)
Clean-label reformulation
Natural source innovation
US footprint expansion
Food safety + labeling compliance
one_sentence: The U.S. natural food coloring manufacturing industry is moving from selective use into mainstream replacement demand as major processors retool products away from petroleum-based dyes through 2026–2027.

title: Natural Gas Liquid Processing
one_liner: U.S. firms that process gas streams into ethane, propane, butane, and natural gasoline are benefiting from sustained upstream gas growth, but still run on highly volatile NGL pricing and export-dependent demand.
overview: In 2025 the U.S. produced 3.941 Tcf of natural gas liquids (NGPL) on a gaseous-equivalent basis, up from 3.659 Tcf in 2024, showing continued growth as shale and associated gas output expands. 2026 data so far (through May, preliminary) is already stronger, with 1.679 Tcf YTD. US NGPL exports reached a record pace in 2025 at 3.1 million b/d, up 7% year-on-year, with ethane and propane leading the volume acceleration. This has reinforced a business model where processors convert feed gas into transportable purity streams, then monetize through fees, fractionation, storage, and export marketing.

key_stats.market_size: 3.941 Tcf NGPL production in 2025 (preliminary, U.S. EIA natural gas monthly table); 3.1 million b/d NGPL exports in 2025 (EIA)
key_stats.growth: 2022→2025 NGPL production growth: +28.2% over three years; 2025 vs 2024 NGPL exports: +7% and 2025 vs 2024 ethane exports: +19%; NGPL export composition remains highly cycle-sensitive to global petrochemical demand

baseline_2022.market_size: 3.075 Tcf NGPL production in 2022 (EIA baseline gas monthly data)

how_it_makes_money: The industry earns mainly through gathering and processing fees for removing NGLs from raw gas, fractionation/segregation fees for purity products, transportation and storage tariffs on dedicated NGL pipelines and caverns, and trading/marketing margins on commodity balancing and spot/term contracts.
cost_structure: High fixed-cost infrastructure base (plants, fractionators, pipelines, storage caverns, marine/export interfaces), substantial energy and compression costs, labor and maintenance intensity, and margin squeeze risk from wide feed gas-to-product spread volatility; capex is lumpy and project-timed rather than smooth.
current_dynamics: The structure is becoming more export-centric around ethane and propane, driven by lower U.S. netback versus parts of Asia and by petrochemical demand, while U.S. production growth in Permian and other basins continues to overload existing fractionation and transport bottlenecks in peak periods.
whats_growing: NGPL output: 2025 total up to 3.941 Tcf from 2024; 2026 May YTD at 1.679 Tcf vs 1.564 Tcf in 2025 YTD.
Global export demand is pulling more US ethane and propane through waterborne channels, helping reset utilization toward higher-value petrochemical-linked destinations.
New and expanded fractionation/pipeline capacity is still being deployed to reduce third-party dependence and capture more downstream spread.
whats_shrinking: Margins remain volatile as NGPL composite and ethane/propane price dispersion compresses around regional supply-demand swings.
Some legacy import pathways are static while export destinations become more concentrated by region and product specification.
Domestic industrial substitution risk persists where power and transport substitution dampens marginal demand for liquid fuels in parts of the broader energy system.
recent_developments: 2026-03-30: EIA reported record 2025 NGPL exports at 3.1 million b/d, up 7% from 2024.
2026-03-30: EIA added that ethane exports rose 92,000 b/d (+19%) in 2025, supported by new cracker demand (including Yantai 2 in China and Coatzacoalcos in Mexico).
2026-07-27: EIA natural gas monthly table reported 2025 annual NGPL at 3.941 Tcf and 2026 Jan–May provisional total at 1.679 Tcf.
2026-08-05: EIA natural gas/NGPL composite price table showed NGPL composite near 7.82 $/MMBtu at Apr-26 with sustained Henry Hub around 2.89 $/MMBtu in Jul-26.
2026-03-31: Targa reported Q1 2026 strong NGL performance, with NGL pipeline transport 1,016.8 MBbl/d and fractionation 1,145.2 MBbl/d, up strongly from Q1 2025.
outlook: Near-term outlook through 2026 remains cautiously positive: production volumes likely keep rising with upstream growth, and export channels stay open, but earnings are expected to remain cyclical and spread-driven. Structural upside is strongest in capacity-backed fractionation and midstream integration; downside risk is tied to global demand repricing and short-cycle commodity spreads.
themes: Export-led NGL growth
Permian-to-ethane cracker linkage
Capacity expansion in fractionation and pipeline systems
Volatility between Henry Hub and NGPL prices
Fee-based infrastructure resilience versus commodity exposure
one_sentence: Natural gas liquid processors are expanding throughput faster than in 2024, while near-term profitability is moderated by commodity swings and heavy fee-based infrastructure costs.

title: Navigational Instrument Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: The U.S. navigational, measuring, electromedical, and control instruments industry is shifting toward FAA and defense-led demand in 2025-26 after earlier volatility.
overview: This industry manufactures navigation, guidance, radar, control, laboratory and process-sensing equipment used across aviation, maritime, energy, healthcare-quality systems, and industrial production. In 2026 the sector is influenced by three major demand engines: FAA airspace modernization, DoD procurement/investment, and industrial automation/measurement spending, while labor and materials costs plus export competition remain key margin pressures.

growth.note: revenue fell 1.7% in 2022 in 2022 baseline report

how_it_makes_money: Sales to public sector programs in defense, navigation/sensor support, and maritime security systems.
Sales to aviation and airport infrastructure projects: radar, ATC communications, surveillance, control and test equipment.
Sales to industrial and laboratory users requiring precision measurement and process-control instrumentation for quality, compliance, and reliability.
Long-tail service revenue from installation, calibration, maintenance, software/firmware support, and lifecycle upgrades.
Technology licensing and integration work tied to mission systems and platform-level avionics solutions.

cost_structure.materials: High due to precision sensors, semiconductors, RF modules, optics, and custom mechanical-electronic assemblies.
cost_structure.labor: High engineering, calibration, QA and integration labor intensity, with skilled technicians and program teams.
cost_structure.R&D: Critical and recurring; firms sustain competitiveness through next-gen navigation, anti-jam resilience, autonomy, and AI/edge capabilities.
cost_structure.compliance: High recurring costs for FAA, MILSPEC, cybersecurity, and quality-regime testing documentation.
cost_structure.servicing: Elevated through field service, support engineering, software updates, and spare parts cycles tied to safety-critical contracts.

current_dynamics: 2025 sectoral output rebounded and was above 2024, indicating demand recovery from broader infrastructure and safety-critical investment cycles.
Labor productivity (output per worker index) improved versus 2022, while employment index remained largely stable in index terms.
FAA modernization spending and controller staffing plans indicate sustained near-term demand for navigation, control, and ATC-adjacent technology.
FY2026 defense budget policy signals significant support for the defense industrial base and sensor/navigation-related modernization programs.
whats_growing: Defense modernization demand linked to aerospace, maritime, and sensor-driven force-structure programs.
FAA air traffic infrastructure modernization and associated terminal control, radar, and communication upgrades.
Higher-value embedded software, autonomy, and diagnostics in industrial/medical-capable instrumentation.
Industry consolidation and capabilities expansion at larger integrators and systems suppliers.
whats_shrinking: Commoditized low-value measurement subassemblies under price pressure from global competitors.
Margins in non-strategic replacement markets where qualification and certification hurdles remain manageable and replacement cycles are shorter.
Short-cycle demand tied to weaker non-essential private capex compared with safety-critical public and defense spend.
recent_developments: 2025-02-12: FAA's FRRM page stated a $8.0bn FY2025–FY2029 FAA facility replacement and radar modernization plan, including $1bn in FY2025 and FY2026 and $2bn in FY2027–FY2029 per year.
2025-06-26: DoD FY2026 budget briefing announced a $1.01tn request request and included explicit defense-industrial-base and high-end munitions, sensors, and modernization investments.
2025-12-04: FAA announced a $12.5bn down payment and an estimated $20bn total requirement for a prime-integrator-led brand-new U.S. air traffic control system program.
2026-05-15: FAA announced $835.8m in ATC facility and contract-tower upgrades, including $85.8m specifically for Federal Contract Towers.
2026-05-15: FAA hiring plan reported 11,000 CPCs deployed and 4,000 in training pipeline, with FY2026 target 2,200 controllers, pointing to sustained ATC expansion.
outlook: For 2026–2027, the industry is likely to remain mildly positive, supported by public-sector modernization spending and defense procurement, while growth is likely uneven across product lines because safety-certified, high-end platforms benefit most and commodity-grade instrumentation faces stronger import and pricing pressure.
themes: Aviation modernization and airspace safety infrastructure
Defense industrial base expansion and sovereign technology supply
Productivity-led manufacturing efficiency
Consolidation toward full-system navigation-sensor integrators
Resilience against import competition and certification costs
one_sentence: US NAICS 3345 output rebounded to about $191.1bn in 2025, with federal infrastructure and defense modernization programs reinforcing demand even as competition and certification-heavy production keep margins under pressure.

title: New Car Dealers in the US
one_liner: U.S. new-car dealer economics are stabilizing after 2025’s price-and-demand volatility, with flat full-year unit growth expected but tighter profit pressure from credit costs and mix shifts.
overview: NADA’s 2025 full-year report shows franchised light-vehicle dealerships selling 16.2M vehicles with $1.3T in total sales, a broad shift toward higher service and parts reliance, and dealer count near 16,990 stores. Inventory normalized around 2.6M units and dealers reported 4.5% average revenue growth, while financing conditions and policy changes are forcing tighter underwriting and stronger fixed-operations focus. By mid-2026, monthly new-vehicle SAAR has rebounded above 16M after a 2026 soft start but remains below the 2025 post-pull-ahead peak, and NADA keeps a full-year 2026 forecast at 16.0M units.

cost_structure.finance_and_credit: Dealer gross margin and close rates are constrained when borrowers face higher contract rates; JD Power cited 2026 July new-vehicle finance rates around 6.54% and rising monthly payments.
cost_structure.floorplan_and_inventory: Inventory remains a major capital drag/benefit variable: New-vehicle on-hand and in-transit inventory stayed near 2.5–2.6M units after tariff and demand normalization.
cost_structure.labor_and_fixed_costs: Labor intensity remains meaningful across sales and fixed ops, with many operators relying on service throughput and parts labor productivity to stabilize profit in a high-rate environment.

major_players: Lithia Motors (455 locations across U.S., U.K., Canada, 2025)
Group 1 Automotive (312 franchises; 2026 public filing footprint)
Penske Automotive Group (365 franchised dealerships; 148 in U.S., 217 overseas, 2025)
Asbury Automotive Group (223 new-vehicle franchises, 171 locations, 15 states)
Sonic Automotive (134 new-vehicle franchises, 111 stores in franchised segment)
current_dynamics: The 2025–2026 cycle is characterized by credit-driven demand moderation, persistent tariff-policy spillovers, and a sharp product-mix pivot toward conventional and plug-in hybrids while BEV momentum cooled after federal EV-credit rollover points. NADA shows dealers using inventory and fixed-operations discipline to offset higher consumer financing costs and slower headline retail new-car growth.
whats_growing: Used-vehicle throughput and used-inventory capture as affordability pressure persists
Service and parts execution (repair, collision, maintenance) as a higher-share profit anchor
Hybrid demand, with market-share gains in 2026 first-half and YTD data
Organic improvement in top dealership groups (fewer pure M&A-led expansions and stronger per-store execution)
whats_shrinking: Early-2026 new-vehicle start-of-year demand weakness (July 2025-level pull-ahead effect faded)
BEV share in June–July 2026, with reported near-term declines versus year-earlier levels
Retail unit growth pace versus 2024–2025 pull-ahead periods, even as absolute level is stabilizing around ~16M
recent_developments: 2025-09: Federal EV tax credits for buyers expired, contributing to September demand timing and a post-peak mix reset (NADA annual report commentary).
2025-09: NADA annual data note 2.5-4%+ tariff effects from imported auto/parts pricing, with new-vehicle inventory ending 2025 around 2.6M units (down 7.6% YoY).
2026-01: NADA Market Beat data showed January SAAR at 14.85M units and inventory at 2.53M units, signaling weaker early-year demand versus prior year.
2026-06: NADA Market Beat reported 16.52M SAAR in June, YTD SAAR 15.9M, plus BEV slowdown and renewed USMCA uncertainty.
2026-07: NADA Market Beat reported 16.3M SAAR in July, with full-year 2026 forecast still at 16.0M despite short-term softness.
outlook: Industry guidance remains for a moderate 2026 with a full-year target near 16.0M units and no immediate rate-relief assumption, so dealer profitability likely depends on mixed-margin balancing between showroom, credit, and fixed-ops performance. The most material upside risk is stronger-than-expected rate easing or demand pull-forward from inventory normalization; downside risk is sustained high rates plus further credit tightening that depresses financed demand.
themes: Credit-rate sensitivity
Hybridization and post-incentive EV-demand reset
Consolidation and top-group execution
Fixed operations as a resilience lever
Policy and trade-policy influence on cost and inventory
one_sentence: The industry in 2025–2026 is dominated by scale networks balancing higher mix risk in new vehicles with stronger used and aftersales reliance while unit growth holds near trend and electrification demand becomes more selective.

title: News Syndicates in the US
one_liner: The US news-syndication market is shrinking in total spend but is being rebuilt around digital-first distribution, video-rich feeds, and AI integration.
overview: This is a declining mature industry where syndicators sell and license text, photo, audio, and video news content rather than owning direct mass audience distribution. The model is pressured by lower print revenues and stronger direct/algorithmic competition from platforms, but supported by persistent demand from broadcasters, digital publishers, and AI systems that need trusted news corpuses. Baseline IBIS logic still points to contraction, while 2025-2026 indicators show faster shifts in where audiences get news and how content is bought.
how_it_makes_money: Primary revenue is from licensing rights to reproduce syndicated text, photos, video, and data across multiple channels, plus premium visual and feature products, custom feeds, and enterprise access deals. In 2025, Associated Press also monetized archive access via partnerships with AI vendors, and syndication licensing was increasingly paired with technology-driven distribution agreements.
cost_structure: Core costs are editorial reporting, bureau operations, and content production (labor-heavy), with rising commercial pressure on fixed staff costs and productivity as automation expands. Variable costs include global rights management, feed/delivery systems, technology integration, and account/custom sales support; margins are constrained by lower print ad-linked demand and price pressure from abundant alternatives.
current_dynamics: Audience behavior in 2025 is strongly digital: 86% of U.S. adults got news from digital devices, while print news readership was down to 7% often. Social platforms continue to capture a large share of news attention, while only about one-third reported AI chatbots as a frequent source. Trust remains volatile, with 2025 data showing declines in confidence in national outlets and continued growth in alternative and creator-led channels.
whats_growing: Demand is shifting toward video-first, mobile-first, and social-distribution-ready packages; enterprise demand is rising for trustworthy data streams and AI-readable news content; and digital ad ecosystems continue to expand, especially social and programmatic channels.
whats_shrinking: Print-oriented demand is structurally weak, with newspaper and consumer magazine advertising and circulation-linked spending under pressure; pay willingness for news remains low for most U.S. adults; and users increasingly bypass traditional gatekeepers through social and creator channels.
recent_developments: 2025-01: AP became the first news publisher to power a Google Gemini AI news flow in Google’s chatbot product.
2025-10: Pew found trust in national news was down 11 percentage points year-over-year in September 2025 (to 56% with some trust).
2025-06: Pew found 83% of U.S. adults had not paid for news in the prior year; only 17% had paid or contributed.
2025: Reuters Institute reported U.S. adults increasingly used social/video networks as primary news source (54%), with news websites/apps at 48%, up from a higher share previously.
2025: IAB estimated US internet advertising rose 13.9% to $294.6bn, while social media ad revenue grew faster at 32.6% in the same period.
outlook: The industry is likely to keep shrinking in aggregate through 2026, but leading operators can hold share by migrating from broad print-linked licensing toward specialized digital, video, and AI-compatible products with tighter account-level offerings. Near-term upside remains in election cycles and enterprise partnerships; downside risks are further ad fragmentation, deep disintermediation by creator ecosystems, and sustained consumer unwillingness to pay.
themes: platform-led consumption replacing channel-led distribution
AI licensing as a separate revenue line
trust and verification as competitive advantage
high-pressure migration from print budgets to digital ad and affiliate models
specialization for niche audiences and local/non-national news coverage
one_sentence: US news syndicates in 2025-2026 face a structurally declining print-backed demand base, while growth pockets are emerging from digital platform licensing, enterprise AI partnerships, and high-frequency news-event demand.
