title: Night Vision Equipment Manufacturing
one_liner: US night-vision makers are pivoting from legacy monocular replacements toward fused, helmet-mounted binocular soldier systems while still relying heavily on defense procurement.
overview: This is a predominantly government-driven manufacturing segment with US military and security programs as the anchor buyer. IBIS baseline shows moderate scale and steady, low-to-mid growth, while current FY2026 budget and 2026 contract announcements show a clear shift toward modular fused-vision soldier programs (BiNOD-style architectures), broader production competition among established primes, and stronger pressure to combine optics, thermal sensing, and software capabilities in one product stack.

key_stats.regional_share: North America accounted for 39.74% of 2025 revenue (US-led demand concentration)
key_stats.government_share: Government customers 63.44% of 2025 revenue; military and defense 57.63% of 2025 share

baseline_2022.market_size: USD 2.55 billion (IBIS-anchored baseline value; nearest 2022 estimate from 2021~USD 2.54 billion and 2021 growth context)
baseline_2022.growth: 0.6% annual growth (2021 baseline trend), with IBIS projecting long-run 1.82% FY2021-2027

how_it_makes_money.revenue_model: Long-cycle defense contracts (development, production, sustainment) and multi-year IDIQ vehicles, plus smaller commercial sales in thermal/security and industrial inspection channels.
how_it_makes_money.pricing: Firm-fixed-price and IDIQ task-order models with lifecycle support, repair, and software-upgrade content.
how_it_makes_money.contract_dependency: High; FY2026 Army and special-operations procurement lines remain major demand drivers.
how_it_makes_money.secondary_revenue: Commercial and critical-infrastructure channels support demand between defense contract spikes.

cost_structure.major_costs: Image intensifier tubes, thermal detector cores, optics, ruggedized housing, and calibration/assembly labor; software stack integration is increasingly material.
cost_structure.cost_pressure: Component cost volatility and qualification cycles for mission-ready optics/electro-optics.
cost_structure.margin_driver: Volume consolidation in common sighting architectures and contract sustainment bundles.
cost_structure.scale_factor: High-volume defense programs can absorb fixed engineering and qualification costs; low-volume legacy replacement sales have thinner margins.

major_players: Elbit Systems / Elbit Systems of America
current_dynamics: FY2026 policy and budgets increased defense totals and re-centered attention on production-ready, networked night-vision suites; competing supplier awards for BiNOD and ENVG-class programs indicate a multi-vendor industrial base rather than single-source dependence.
whats_growing: Fused, helmet-mounted binocular soldier systems (networked thermal + image intensification).
Commercial surveillance/security deployments using lower-cost thermal imaging and AI inference.
Domestic US manufacturing footprint and local testing/production capacity within U.S.-facing suppliers.
whats_shrinking: Direct legacy monocular replacement spend where fused binocular fielding is now prioritized.
Pure hardware-only competition that does not include sustainment, software, and integration elements.
recent_developments: 2026-03-02: Exosens/Photonis awarded a US Army BiNOD firm-fixed-price IDIQ with a US$352.6 million ceiling through 2033.
2026-04-13: L3Harris won a U.S. Army seven-year BiNOD-related award with potential value up to US$465 million.
2026-05-01: Elbit Systems of America received an Army contract for BiNOD development and testing, linked to up to US$450.6 million future production opportunity.
2026-05-12: Elbit received a US$212 million delivery order for ENVG-B binocular production support.
2026-01-28: Elbit received approximately US$74.4 million in SBNVG delivery orders for the Marine Corps through 2027.
2025-09-02: Teledyne FLIR launched the Boson+ IQ thermal imaging development kit, signaling stronger low-cost AI-integrated thermal ecosystems.
outlook: Moderate growth should continue into 2026-2027 as defense modernization and border/security applications stay active, but supplier competition and cost pressure will stay high. Watch whether federal procurement shifts further toward modular common-sensor standards and whether commercial demand can offset cyclical defense pacing.
themes: BiNOD-class modularity
fused night-vision architectures
DoD budget-linked program continuity
industrial base localization in optics and imaging
AI-enabled thermal analytics adoption
competition across contract, sustainment, and ecosystem value
one_sentence: In 2025–2026, US night-vision demand is being reshaped by defense re-modernization programs and faster commercialization of thermal imaging into commercial security and mobility use cases.

title: Non-Hotel Casinos in the US
one_liner: US non-hotel casinos are stand-alone gaming properties that separate slot and table game play from lodging while competing with expanding sports wagering and online casino channels.
overview: The segment has recovered from the pandemic-era weakness and is now benefiting from broader commercial gaming expansion, while remaining a subset of the larger casino market that is increasingly driven by cross-channel behavior. In this format, margins depend on managing floor mix, customer frequency, and cost discipline as players shift between physical casinos and regulated online alternatives.

growth.note: From 19.831 billion USD in 2022 to 22.7 billion USD in 2024 using non-hotel casino series references

market_size.source_metric: Total Revenue for Casinos Excluding Casino Hotels, Employer Firms

how_it_makes_money: Earns gaming revenue from slot machines, table games, and wagering products at stand-alone facilities and riverboat/"dockside" formats.
Adds incremental income through food and beverage, promotions, entertainment programming, and limited hospitality upsells without full casino hotel packages.
Uses sports-betting and iGaming-adjacent customer relationships to increase visit frequency and cross-property spend.
cost_structure: High fixed overhead for gaming floor operations, surveillance, security, cash handling, and floor labor
Ongoing hardware/software spend for slot systems, authentication, and age/geo/compliance controls
Regulatory and licensing costs across state jurisdictions, plus tax and fee obligations tied to gaming revenue
Property and lease costs are elevated where operations are third-party-realty driven
Marketing and customer acquisition spending intensified by online and sports-betting competitors
current_dynamics: Non-hotel casinos are operating inside a faster-growing commercial gaming system where 2025 nationwide U.S. commercial GGR reached 78.72 billion USD (press release, 2026-02-26).

Sports-betting and iGaming are the strongest momentum engines: 2025 sports betting was 16.96 billion USD and iGaming was 10.74 billion USD (+22.8% and +27.6% respectively versus 2024 in AGA reporting context).
In 2025, total traditional land-based commercial GGR rose to 51.06 billion USD, showing physical slots/table-game demand is stabilizing rather than collapsing.
Record-setting jurisdiction performance in 2024 and 2025 increased competitive pressure for non-hotel operators to defend footfall versus larger integrated destinations.
whats_growing: Regulated sports betting ecosystems and online casino revenue continue to accelerate, with Maine-style policy adoption and multi-market expansion extending distribution
Cross-channel monetization through mobile offers, in-venue loyalty ecosystems, and sportsbook funnels at stand-alone locations
Municipal and state dependence on gaming tax receipts, which supports incremental political support for regulated product expansion
whats_shrinking: Relative appeal of isolated stand-alone locations versus casino resorts with hotels/entertainment ecosystems
Share of local spend captured by non-hotel formats versus unbundled digital substitutes among younger players
Policy and enforcement risk from unregulated/sweepstakes or offshore alternatives reducing legal capture in some states
recent_developments: 2025-05-13: AGA State of the States 2025 reported 2024 commercial gaming revenue at 72.04 billion USD, up 7.5% y/y.
2025-05-13: AGA noted NC and Vermont launched regulated mobile sports betting in 2024 and reported first-time commercial sports-betting impact.
2025-05-13: AGA reported 2024 non-tribal iGaming from seven legal states reached 8.41 billion USD (+28.7%).
2026-02-26: AGA press release said 2025 commercial GGR reached 78.72 billion USD (+9.2%), with 18.09 billion USD in gaming taxes.
2026-05-12: State of the States 2026 reported 2025 iGaming at 10.73 billion USD (+27.6%), while 34 states + D.C. set revenue records.
outlook: Near-term outlook is positive but uneven: non-hotel operators should benefit as 2025-era monetization from sports betting and iGaming lifts overall patronage, while pressure persists from integrated resort alternatives and substitute digital channels unless facilities improve non-hotel entertainment and day-visit conversion.
themes: Convergence of brick-and-mortar and digital wagering funnels
Regulatory expansion into adjacent betting markets
Competition with online/portable gaming products
Market concentration around jurisdictions with active tax-sensitive gaming ecosystems
Operational modernization through higher automation and rightsized labor
one_sentence: Demand in 2025 remained strong as regulated betting ecosystems lifted casino spend, but operator economics for non-hotel formats stayed vulnerable to hotel-casino and digital competition.

title: Nondestructive Testing Services
one_liner: US NDT services use non-destructive inspection techniques to keep critical assets safe, with demand rising from tighter lifecycle, inspection, and infrastructure reliability requirements.
overview: US demand is concentrated in oil and gas, power generation, industrial processing, and aerospace/defense, where inspections are mandatory for safety and reliability. The industry is increasingly shifting from traditional manual workflows toward automated and data-rich inspection programs, including remote sensing, drones, and AI-assisted defect interpretation, but labor depth and certification requirements remain a structural constraint.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: USD 3.952 billion (US NDT and inspection market, according to 2025 baseline source)
key_stats.service_anchoring: Services remain the major revenue stream; inspection services led segment in 2024 with over 50% share in broader US NDT service estimates

baseline_2022.growth: 2022-2025: 4.2% CAGR proxy (using 2025 value above and 2022 reported baseline estimate)

how_it_makes_money: Inspection project fees and recurring asset-integrity contracts (pipeline, pressure equipment, structural and aerospace components)
Higher-margin advanced testing modes (advanced radiography, phased-array ultrasonic, digital analysis, robotics-enabled field inspections)
Supplementary services such as repair planning support, digital reporting, and compliance documentation tied to regulated industries
cost_structure: Labor remains the dominant cost base because skilled certification, field deployment, and review effort are intensive; wage pressure is amplified by specialist scarcity. Equipment, software platforms, and travel/logistics are important but scale with project intensity and specialization. Major players also incur rising SG&A and reclassification-related cost shifts linked to staffing and quality infrastructure.

supporting_factors: 2025-2026 pipeline safety rule activity increased inspection and leak-detection compliance requirements
Aerospace and industrial safety directives continue to reinforce mandatory defect and corrosion surveillance
Major operators are expanding digital inspection portfolios and software-backed reporting for auditability and faster closeout
pressures: Regulatory scope creates sustained demand but also requires high certification discipline and documentation burden
Service capacity remains constrained by experienced Level II/III technician depth and training throughput
Commodity and energy capex cycles can still produce uneven quarterly demand

whats_growing: AI-assisted defect classification and automated ultrasonic/radiographic workflows
Remote sensing and drone-enabled right-of-way or above-ground inspection methods in high-risk infrastructure corridors
Recurring compliance-linked asset integrity contracts in energy, pipeline, and industrial asset portfolios
Data integrity, digital evidence packages, and condition-monitoring add-ons around core testing
whats_shrinking: Simple purely manual routine checks where automated platforms can substitute
Single-use legacy analog process workflows with limited data capture
Projects delayed by lower industrial activity in cyclical segments during macro pullbacks
recent_developments: 2025-10-02: PHMSA published rulemaking entries including remote-sensing-based right-of-way patrol language for gas and hazardous liquid pipelines
2025-01-17: PHMSA posted a final-rule leak-detection and repair package requiring stronger leak surveys and recordkeeping for gas operators
2026-04-24: PHMSA issued additional pipeline-safety rule activity in the Federal Register, including pipeline incident and documentation updates
2026-03-04: MISTRAS reported Q4 and FY2025 results with revenue of USD 724.0 million and improved EBITDA performance
2026-03-04: MISTRAS attributed 2025 profitability improvement to demand in end markets plus stronger digital inspection, integrity, and talent capabilities
outlook: From 2026 into 2030, the most likely path is moderate-to-strong expansion with continued replacement of manual processes by automated NDT, stronger regulatory-driven recurring programs, and consolidation around operators that can pair field execution with advanced data products.
themes: Asset integrity and regulatory compliance as recurring demand engines
Shift from basic inspection to digital NDT platforms
Pipeline and industrial safety modernization
Skilled labor scarcity and certification intensity
Consolidation around full-lifecycle service providers
one_sentence: The US NDT services market in 2025 is entering a recovery path, supported by stricter pipeline and aviation compliance activity and by broader adoption of digital, automated inspection workflows.

title: Nonferrous Metal Foundry Products Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: US nonferrous foundries cast aluminum and other light metals into components for vehicles, aircraft, defense, energy, and industrial equipment.
overview: The US nonferrous foundry sector serves transportation and aerospace most heavily, with additional exposure to industrial machinery and infrastructure-linked applications. After a weak 2024 in many segments, AFS reported a 2025 sales rebound and renewed 2026 optimism, but foundries still face shortages, tariff effects, and energy/logistics cost pressure.

growth.2026: AFS projected +4.2% in 2026; January to June 2026 survey signal in Q2 showed strong order/momentum despite shortages

market_size.source_note: Used as the most recent explicit IBIS nonferrous foundry baseline in the 2022 update

how_it_makes_money: Foundries generate revenue by supplying castings to downstream OEMs, usually via contracts that blend tonnage volume, alloy mix, and price adjustment clauses linked to commodity indexes; many nonferrous casthouses pass through part of aluminum premium moves to customers.

cost_structure.details: Aluminum and alloy inputs are the dominant cost driver; a 2025 filing by Alcoa reported aluminum prices up 9% y/y and noted pricing in products is linked to LME P1020 aluminum plus regional and negotiated premiums.
AFS Q2 2026 survey: 98% of foundries still reported worker shortages; 55% planned headcount increases.
US industrial electricity price in May 2026 was 8.71 cents/kWh vs 8.29 in May 2025 (EIA).
AFS Q2 2026 survey reported 88% of foundries saw freight costs rising.
Tariff, permit, and regulatory uncertainty remain significant, with rising import-duty-related premiums and varying compliance costs affecting order economics.

major_players: Allegheny Technologies, Inc. (competitive set in precision castings/materials)

current_dynamics.demand: Automotive electrification and aerospace engine/structural demand are stabilizing orderbooks versus prior-year weakness.
current_dynamics.investment: AFS reported broad reinvestment: >90% of foundries made capital investments in 2025 and 95% in 2026.
current_dynamics.sourcing: Reshoring activity is increasing while price/tariff pressure is raising cost and qualification complexity.
current_dynamics.productivity: AFS Q2 2026 foundries showed higher confidence and net-positive order expectations, with most participants expecting tonnage growth.

whats_growing: 2025-2026 increase in casting demand in automotive and power/defense-linked programs, reflected in AFS +1.9% (2025) and +4.2% (2026) sales assumptions.
Automation and digitalization (AFS Q2 2026 reports 43% piloting/evaluating AI).
Reshoring and onshoring activity in North America and defense-related procurement.
EV and e-mobility applications in aluminum/structural castings, including battery-related assemblies and chassis/lightweight structures.
whats_shrinking: Some foundry orderbooks remain under pressure (Q2 2026 still had lower sales expectations at a meaningful minority of respondents).
Offshore and tariff-sensitive competitiveness is squeezing price-to-cost conversion.
Substitution and value-based design pressure in certain end uses, especially plumbing/valve segments with alternative materials.
recent_developments: 2025-07-22: AFS projected 2025 casting sales growth of 1.9% and said most foundries faced easing inflation pressure versus 2021-2022.
2026-03-17: AFS March 2026 survey reported 72% positive outlook for 2026 and more than half of respondents with rising sales in the prior 90 days.
2026-Q2: AFS Metalcasters Outlook reported a Metalcasting Sentiment Index of 75.0 and 55% headcount increase expectations with 98% still reporting labor shortages.
2026-07-23 (EIA data release): U.S. industrial electricity averaged 8.71 cents/kWh in May 2026 versus 8.29 cents/kWh in May 2025.
2025 (SEC filing): Alcoa reported aluminum prices up 9% year-over-year, with Midwest premium up 211% partly tied to tariff movements on North American aluminum imports.
outlook: Near-term outlook is constructive on volume but mixed on margins: demand from transportation, aerospace, and infrastructure could support continued revenue growth through 2026-2027 if policy uncertainty stabilizes, while margin recovery depends on how quickly raw materials, freight, and labor costs moderate.
themes: policy-driven regionalization
energy and logistics inflation
talent scarcity in foundry operations
automation and AI-assisted production planning
lightweighting and electrification demand
one_sentence: The industry is cyclical and materials-driven, with demand tied to transportation and industrial retooling while labor, freight, and raw-metal costs remain major margin pressure points.

title: Nonferrous Metal Recycling
one_liner: US nonferrous metal recycling is consolidating around higher scrap recovery, stricter cross-border controls, and tariff-driven domestic content demand.
overview: The US nonferrous recycling chain remains a key secondary-metal gateway for manufacturing, packaging, and mobility sectors. Industry activity is led by aluminum- and copper-centric flows, with recycling increasingly favored because recycled material keeps energy use low versus primary production. In 2024, U.S. aluminum recovered from purchased scrap was about 3.6 million tons, and in 2024 copper recycling supplied about 35% of apparent copper supply, indicating heavy dependence on scrap economics. Demand remained resilient in 2025 as downstream manufacturing and vehicle and transport supply chains stabilized, while policy changes raised compliance and sourcing complexity.

baseline_2022.note: The provided baseline text uses 2021 baseline markers and 2021-27 projections; no explicit standalone 2022 total-revenue figure was exposed in the file.

how_it_makes_money: Purchases metal scrap from industrial generators (new/in-process and old/discarded products).
Sorts, preprocesses, and remelts/dumps into secondary metal into forms used by converters, roll mills, foundries, and fabricators.
Sells recovered metal, alloying charges, and processed material to automotive, construction, electrical, machinery, and packaging supply chains.
Captures trading and logistics margins in brokered and processed transactions where spread and inventory turns matter most.
cost_structure: Commodity-cost pass-through: spent-metal procurement and inbound logistics are the largest variable costs.
Energy intensity in smelting, melting, and casting operations.
Sort/separation, cutting, and processing costs, including equipment wear and maintenance.
Inventory carrying, hedging, and price-risk management for volatile metal spreads.
Environmental, permitting, and compliance costs (including hazardous-metal handling, trade documentation, and security-related requirements).
major_players: Sims Limited (global metal recycling leader; FY25 sales 7,494 million USD)
Novelis (world leader in aluminum rolling and recycling; FY25 net sales 17.1 billion USD)
OmniSource (Metal recycling operator; wholly owned subsidiary of Steel Dynamics)
Nucor via DJJ raw-materials operations (major scrap brokerage/recycling platform in the US)
current_dynamics: 2025-2026 is characterized by stronger scrap-policy friction and demand recovery: recycled metal flows are supported by higher near-term output demand in transportation and packaging, while import-duty and trade-control changes are pushing buyers toward domestic scrap availability and certified material. 2026 tariff changes increased the economics of reliable U.S.-origin feed and added documentation pressure for mixed-metal products. Simultaneously, Basel-based controls on electrical and electronic scrap exports/imports are increasing trade friction and increasing due diligence around sourcing from e-waste channels.
whats_growing: Recycled aluminum inputs in automotive and packaging demand chains.
Recycled copper availability tied to brass, wire-rod, and consumer-eletromechanical recycling
Capacity utilization and capex for secondary processing in the US in response to higher material security concerns.
whats_shrinking: Unplanned export arbitrage opportunities for low-cost e-scrap and mixed-metal flows under tighter documentation.
Margins in periods of volatile scrap vs remelt price spreads unless hedged and integrated.
Small fragmented processors with limited compliance capability and financing.
recent_developments: 2025-01-01: EPA reported Basel electronic and electrical waste amendments entered into effect, requiring prior written consent controls on many e-waste and scrap shipments.
2025-05-18: Aluminum Association reported North American aluminum demand in 2025 at 26.65 billion pounds (+0.8% from 2024), with scrap inventory up 18.6%.
2025-09-24: Novelis announced FY2025 sustainability outcomes, including 63% average recycled content in products and >84 billion used beverage cans recycled.
2026-04-06: White House presidential action took effect strengthening Section 232 duty treatment for aluminum/steel/copper imports, with high base ad valorem rates depending on origin and content.
2026-07-20: White House signaled further aluminum-duty and primary-smelter investment incentives, including reduced rates for approved onshoring plans.
outlook: Medium-term demand is constructive as EV adoption, infrastructure activity, and lightweight transport use-cases keep nonferrous secondary demand elevated. Near-term performance remains sensitive to tariff administration, freight and energy costs, and the quality of imported scrap availability. Industry structure is likely to remain consolidated, with fewer, larger processors advantaged by compliance and scale.
themes: Decarbonization economics accelerate recycled-content mandates.
Section 232 tariff regime shifts reinforce domestic scrap value.
Trade-compliance pressure increases for e-waste and mixed-metal imports.
EV/energy-transition demand supports aluminum/copper recycling throughput.
Operational concentration continues, favoring integrated processors with downstream offtake integration.
one_sentence: The sector recovers aluminum, copper, and related nonferrous streams from industrial and post-consumer scrap, with margin increasingly tied to commodity spread management and recycled-feed availability.

title: Nonferrous Metal Refining in the US
one_liner: The US nonferrous metal refining system in 2025–26 is small, concentrated, and exposed to volatile metal prices and import dependence despite stronger policy focus on domestic critical-mineral supply.
overview: USGS’s 2026 Mineral Commodity Summaries and monthly industry surveys show a structurally narrow U.S. nonferrous refining base: production is increasingly tied to a small number of primary smelters and refineries, while downstream manufacturing demand remains linked to construction, electronics, transportation, and defense/energy infrastructure. The industry remains highly exposed to policy, tariff, and trade shifts, with critical-mineral designations and new environmental controls raising the cost of operation and permitting pressure. Refining economics continue to depend more on refining margins and feedstock resilience than on commodity scarcity alone.

key_stats.market_size: USGS MCS 2026 indicates domestic mine production value for copper in 2025 was estimated at $11.0 billion, and the same report documents a narrowed U.S. copper processing base (e.g., 2 primary smelters and 2 secondary smelters) with 4 primary/refining channels in active use; lead annual refined output in the US was around 1.41 million metric tons.
key_stats.growth: In 2025, U.S. mine recoverable copper fell 5% while mine value rose 10%; domestic refined copper was reported to be about 9% lower than 2024 due planned maintenance at primary smelters; U.S. lead data showed mine recoverable output weaker in some months but sustained secondary processing volumes.

baseline_2022.market_size: USGS/IBISWorld baseline for this industry: $15,723 million revenue (2022)
baseline_2022.growth: IBISWorld growth baseline: 6.4% CAGR (2017-2022) with 0.18% projected CAGR to 2028

how_it_makes_money: The sector makes money by buying/processing primary ore concentrates and secondary scrap streams, running smelting and refining (electrolytic and electrowon pathways), producing refined copper/lead/zinc/molybdenum products and alloys, and selling outputs into construction, wiring, automotive, power, electronics, industrial machinery, and battery-related demand channels. Revenue quality is highly sensitive to metal spread between input concentrate/feed stock and refined product realizations.

cost_structure.capital: Very high fixed capital from smelters/refineries, periodic outages, and long-cycle maintenance.
cost_structure.energy_and_chemicals: High electricity and fuel intensity in furnaces and electrorefining; variable reagent and sulfur/roasting cost exposure.
cost_structure.compliance: EPA hazardous-air and emissions obligations (including secondary lead smelting NESHAP updates) increase monitoring, reporting, and control system costs.
cost_structure.compliance_risk: Environmental permitting, waste handling, and inventory controls remain major fixed and variable obligations in permit-constrained districts.
cost_structure.commodity: Revenue and margin are highly tied to global copper and lead price cycles, including processed material value swings.

major_players: Freeport-McMoRan (major U.S. copper mine, smelting and refining operator; claims dominant refined-share positioning in its company disclosures)
Rio Tinto Kennecott (integrated Utah mine-smelter-refinery operation; one of only two operating U.S. copper smelters per company disclosure)
Grupo México / ASARCO (U.S. smelting and refining footprint around Hayden smelter and Amarillo processing assets, with announced expansion/restart deliberations in 2025–26)
U.S. secondary lead smelting sector (11 facilities in EPA’s Secondary Lead Smelting NESHAP source category, four of which are in small-business ownership)
current_dynamics: Copper mine output in 2025 showed value resilience despite tonnage softness; recovered mine tonnage fell while value increased on price.
Domestic refined copper volume is constrained by planned maintenance and limited primary smelting throughput despite high global demand signals.
Lead refining shows a dual-channel dynamic: small domestic mine base, large secondary scrap-based refinery processing, and net export/import dependence in unwrought lead streams.
Critical-mineral policy has shifted incentives toward domestic processing, while imports of processed metals and materials remain very high.
EPA technical review and modernization of secondary lead NESHAP rules is adding permitting and emissions-management complexity.
whats_growing: Electrowon and secondary recovery pathways remain important where primary ore availability is constrained.
Domestic critical-mineral framing has strengthened investment rationale for integrated production-to-refining projects.
Downstream demand from EVs, digital infrastructure, and construction-related wiring/electrical systems remains a stabilizing long-cycle demand signal.
Company-level modernization/expansion announcements around existing U.S. assets are increasing throughput ambition despite capacity limits.
whats_shrinking: Domestic refined copper output declined year-over-year in 2025 due smelter maintenance effects.
Mine recoverable copper output trended down in 2025 as ore- and grade-related constraints persisted.
Industry structure remains concentration-prone with only a few active U.S. primary smelting/refining channels.
Import dependence for processed metals materials remains material, with import-led exposure rising in value terms across the broader mineral chain.
recent_developments: 2026-02-06: USGS released Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026, with total US mineral production up 5.6% in 2025 and net imports of processed metals/materials up to $185 billion versus $77 billion in 2024.
2025-11-07: USGS Final 2025 List of Critical Minerals added 60 minerals, including copper, silver, lead, tellurium and others, reinforcing critical-supply priorities.
2025-09-29: EPA issued a proposed revision to Secondary Lead Smelting NESHAP (40 CFR Part 63) for 11 secondary lead smelters; proposal opens a major compliance cycle.
2025-07-30: Reuters (via market-report host) reported Grupo México reassessing U.S. expansion and potential Hayden smelter restart amid tariff regime changes.
outlook: Near-term outlook is mixed: higher price-to-cost transmission for some outputs is likely to support margins, but near-term throughput upside is constrained by concentrated primary smelter capacity and maintenance cycles. Policy support may continue for domestic value retention, yet import reliance and emissions-compliance obligations keep margin expansion uneven until capacity expansion and permitting clear materially.
themes: Capacity concentration and maintenance-driven volatility
Critical minerals policy and import-security framing
Air toxics and environmental compliance intensity
Shift toward integrated mining-to-refining chains
High sensitivity to metal price cycles and trade policy
one_sentence: US nonferrous refining is entering 2026 with higher upstream mine value but tighter domestic throughput, continued import exposure, and rising compliance complexity.

title: Nonferrous Metal Rolling & Alloying in the US
one_liner: A mature, high-sensitivity US alloys industry is increasingly shifting from broad commodity output toward aerospace-grade, high-performance nonferrous rolling, drawing, and extruding solutions.
overview: The US NAICS 331491 segment produces rolled, drawn, extruded and alloyed nonferrous shapes excluding copper and aluminum, serving aerospace, industrial machinery, energy, transportation, and electronics supply chains. The segment is structurally smaller than it was in the pre-pandemic expansion period, with near-term demand tied to recovery in aircraft manufacturing and certified engine/airframe supply; long-term demand supports by defense and energy decarbonization equipment.

key_stats.market_size: 2022 baseline: $18,529m industry revenue; 2026 proxy activity: NAICS 331491 PPI = 254.493 (Dec 2003=100) and NAICS 331491 output index in FRED table = 254.493 (Dec 2003=100), with 2025 import-price index level at 142.2 (IZ33149, Dec 2021=100).
key_stats.growth: 2026: nonferrous 33149 PPI rose 1.5% from Feb 2026 (250.804) to Jun 2026 (254.493); 2026 industrial-production row shows 2025→2026 Jun year-over-year output index +5.4% (241.331 to 254.493).

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: $18,529m revenue; imports $20,909m; exports $8,402m; NAICS 33149 value-added in 2022: $6,768m (Federal Reserve Industry Structure table).
baseline_2022.growth: 2003-2022 revenue CAGR: +3.10%; projected 2022-2028 revenue CAGR: +0.41%; exports projected CAGR 2022-2028: +0.95%; imports projected CAGR 2022-2028: -1.64%.

how_it_makes_money: Revenue is driven by value-added processing of nonferrous metal shapes and alloys sold to aerospace/defense, energy, and industrial customers, with pricing tied to raw-material costs through contractual arrangements. ATI’s 2025 filing shows aerospace and defense became a large revenue share (41%) and rising via long-term sales with major OEMs, illustrating the importance of qualified long-cycle aerospace contracts.

cost_structure.raw_materials: Critical inputs are high-concentration (nickel, titanium, zirconium, cobalt, molybdenum, etc.), and 2025 import-price data for NAICS 331490 shows index strength (118.5 in Jan 2025 to 142.2 in Jun 2025), indicating persistent material-cost pressure.
cost_structure.labor: 2026 BLS primary metal manufacturing data show rising pay pressure (all employees: $37.44/hour in Jul 2026) and about 367k workers in Apr-Jun 2026; labor and skill intensity remains meaningful for specialty alloy operations.
cost_structure.pricing: PPI by industry climbed from Feb 2026 to Jun 2026, and fixed-price arrangements with change-in-cost clauses make earnings sensitive to raw-material and process-cost volatility.

current_dynamics: The segment is balancing slower recovery in broad transport demand with stronger pull from aerospace engine/airframe programs and policy-backed domestic critical-mineral resilience. FAA materials constraints reduced widebody deliveries in 2025 (233 vs 403 in 2019), while policy actions in 2026 targeted processed critical mineral security, and DOE announced expanded domestic critical-mineral recycling and workforce programs.
whats_growing: 2025-2026 aerospace demand quality: FAA forecasts show aircraft production capacity constraints unwind slowly, and major OEM demand cycles continue to prioritize high-performance metal solutions.
Aerospace and defense mix expansion: ATI reported 2025 aerospace & defense sales up, helping support premium alloy demand.
Domestic recycling/supply-chain recovery: DOE programs in 2026 and policy focus on domestic critical-mineral processing/support are improving near-term capex for recovery and reprocessing.
whats_shrinking: Volatility rather than sustained broad expansion: widebody manufacturing remains constrained, and legacy cyclical sectors (industrial and some energy-use cases) remain uneven by region.
Margin headroom versus inflation: raw-material and freight volatility in key metals plus elevated compliance/security-related supply fragility keep structural margin risk high.
Imported critical feedstock dependence: policy responses indicate persistent concern that foreign concentration can still constrain cost and availability.
recent_developments: 2025: FAA forecast cites global widebody deliveries of 233 in 2025 vs 403 in 2019, reflecting ongoing production constraints.
2026-01-14: White House announced 232 actions to negotiate processed critical mineral import controls (with national-security framing and 180-day escalation authority).
2026-03-31: Boeing’s March 2026 8-K disclosed backlog rose from $567,290m (2025 year-end) to $575,583m, while airline and production bottlenecks persist.
2026-06-02: DOE announced $134m to support domestic rare-earth recovery from waste and partnerships for critical materials.
2026-07-17: FAA confirmed resumed 737 MAX/787 certifications after safety-review-related production delays resumed.
2026-08-07: DOE announced $100m to build the US critical minerals workforce and strengthen domestic supply chains.
outlook: Outlook is moderate upside rather than sharp growth: output and demand proxies suggest a gradual recovery path through 2027, but earnings remain sensitive to aerospace cycle normalization, imported material costs, and geopolitical/raw-material policy shocks. The strongest demand likely remains in high-value aerospace, turbine, and mission-critical alloy platforms.
themes: Shift from commodity output to engineered high-value alloying
Critical-mineral security and domestic processing depth as competitiveness levers
Aerospace bottleneck relief translating to selective demand acceleration
Material-price volatility management through longer contracts and mix upgrade
Recycling and circular feedstock adoption to reduce imported input exposure
one_sentence: US nonferrous metal rolling and alloying in 2026 is driven by slower but stabilizing aerospace and critical-minerals policy dynamics, while still exposed to raw-material price swings and global supply-chain volatility.

title: Nuclear Power in the US
one_liner: U.S. nuclear power remains a large, low-carbon baseload asset with flat-to-slightly rising near-term output, while long-asset aging, slower reactor approvals, and cost competition with gas/renewables keep structural growth muted.
overview: The U.S. industry is still concentrated around a mature fleet of legacy sites; as of March 2026 it had 96 reactors at 57 plants, and capacity has been held up through plant uprates and operational efficiency rather than broad greenfield additions. Nuclear generation still holds a meaningful role in grid reliability, but share pressure is visible in the broader power mix outlook.

key_stats.market_size: U.S. utility-scale nuclear generation was about 225.253 TWh in 2025 (preliminary, EIA utility generation table) and about 18% of total utility-scale U.S. generation in 2025 (about 4.43 TWh total), equal to roughly 0.797 TWh in utility-scale share framing.
key_stats.growth: Preliminary EIA utility generation rose from 220.163 TWh in 2024 to 225.253 TWh in 2025 (+2.3%); January–May 2026 nuclear utility generation was 183.991 TWh annualized-to-date, indicating normalization and weather/operational variation effects.
key_stats.fuel_mix_context: Iodized toward higher-cost dispatch competition from cheap gas and falling costs in wind and solar; NRC safety and decommissioning timelines remain a binding planning factor.

how_it_makes_money: Bulk of revenue is from electricity generation sold to utilities, industrial customers, and wholesale power markets.
Margin upside depends on plant availability, capacity factor, and fuel cost control across long-lived assets.
Most operators monetize fixed-asset intensity over decades through stable baseload contracts and utility-scale dispatch revenue.
Long horizon of existing assets enables lifecycle cost recovery through decommissioning, life-extension, and uprate-driven output gains.
cost_structure: High fixed O&M and capital recovery burden; long lead-cycle plants are maintenance- and compliance-intensive.
Fuel is a major variable cost driver, with uranium price volatility affecting generation economics.
Safety and regulatory compliance costs (NRC reporting, inspections, outage management, decommissioning trust obligations) are structurally embedded in cost profile.
Nuclear power is highly capital intensive but relatively low variable cost once operational, making dispatch economics sensitive to gas-price and renewables-capex dynamics.
Long-term uranium contracts continue to dominate procurement, while spot exposure remains a risk management focus.
major_players: Duke Energy Carolinas / Duke Energy Progress
APS / Arizona Public Service and regional joint-venture owners
current_dynamics: Near-term output growth is mostly from uprates rather than large new reactor deployment.
Federal support has intensified for advanced reactor deployment (R&D and early commercial pathways).
Licensing and safety oversight cadence remains lengthy, but regulatory modernization is progressing.
The policy narrative is stronger for nuclear as a reliability and decarbonization enabler, even as market share faces competitive pressure.
Industry mix is shifting toward fewer older units, more life-extended operations, and selective modernization.
whats_growing: Advanced reactor policy support, including SMR pathway and commercialization pilots.
License applications and design certifications for modular and non-light-water concepts.
Selective capacity uprates and life-extension projects on existing nuclear sites.
Grid- resilience policy arguments that favor firm baseload and firming capability.
whats_shrinking: Net market share in long-run AEO framing, with nuclear generation share expected to drift lower versus natural gas, wind, and solar without stronger policy intensity.
New large single-unit build volume, excluding the last AP1000 in-service phase and isolated new-construction cases.
Relative flexibility compared with modular renewables and fast gas-cycle economics in many regions.
recent_developments: 2025-05-29: NRC approved the NuScale US460 standard design for small modular reactors.
2025-05-20: TVA submitted the second and final part of the Clinch River SMR construction permit package to NRC.
2025-12-?: DOE structured a $900M SMR solicitation and selected $800M Tier 1 path projects for early Tennessee/Michigan SMR deployments.
2026-05-14: DOE announced more than $94M for eight companies to support US Gen III+ SMR deployment readiness.
2026-07-?: NRC announced first non-light-water reactor construction approval (TerraPower permitting milestone), highlighting regulatory movement into advanced reactor classes.
2026-03-?: EIA reported 96 operating commercial nuclear reactors at 57 plants, with 98,441 MW net summer capacity.
outlook: Near term, U.S. nuclear appears operationally stable but strategically transitional: modest near-term generation growth from utilization actions, while long-run shares are likely to stay pressured without sustained policy, financing, and manufacturing support. EIA’s long-range framing shows nuclear share falling to roughly 12–15% by 2050 in baseline scenarios, but policy-led acceleration around advanced reactors and domestic supply chains could materially alter that trajectory before the 2030s.
themes: Uprates and life-extension as bridge strategy for an aging fleet
Advanced reactors/SMRs moving from design-to-construction pipeline
Security of uranium supply and fuel-cycle resilience
Grid reliability and emissions policy increasingly favorable to dispatchable generation
Regulatory throughput as both hurdle and enabler
one_sentence: The sector is transitioning from a mature large-reactor base toward uprates, selective life-extension, and early advanced-small modular reactor commercialization supported by federal policy and licensing momentum.

title: Nursery & Garden Stores in the US
one_liner: US nursery and garden retailers remain in a mature but resilient niche, balancing local-service advantage against aggressive price pressure from large home-improvement chains.
overview: IBISWorld’s 2022 baseline places the sector at 42,286 million USD in revenue with a 4.4% profit margin and a 54.9% mix from farm/agricultural supplies. In 2025, broader NAICS 44422 output data available from FRED shows 54,443.269 million USD (not seasonally adjusted), indicating a higher nominal activity base but with definitional differences versus IBIS revenue. In 2025-26, competitive intensity from Home Depot, Lowe’s, and related omnichannel chains has increased, while consumer demand for garden and lawn products remains supported by home improvement and lifestyle spending.

market_size.definition: Sectoral output for NAICS 44422 (Retail Trade: Nursery, Garden Center, and Farm Supply Stores), FRED

how_it_makes_money: Primary retail sales of nursery stock, plants, seeds, bulbs, soil, sod, and small farm/lawn consumables.
Secondary sales of hardware, tools, fertilizers, fuels, and farm inputs (especially where regional gardening and DIY demand is strong).
Service differentiation through in-store guidance and small-batch/specialty product curation to reduce substitution to big-box formats.
Seasonal and recurring demand around spring/summer planting, home improvement cycles, and property upgrade projects.

2025_2026_evidence: Home Depot FY2025 SG&A 30.7 billion USD, 18.6% of net sales.
Tractor Supply FY2025 SG&A was 27.0% of net sales, higher than prior-year 26.4%.
Fertilizer, fuel, and delivery costs are repeatedly noted as pressure points in sector and peer disclosures.
Tractor Supply Q4/FY2025 commentary highlighted transportation cost increases as a margin drag.
Large chains investing in interconnected fulfillment options and store distribution footprints create structural cost competition.
Lowes and Home Depot continue to expand integrated fulfillment and private-label operations, raising category benchmark expectations.

title: Nursery Schools
one_liner: Enrollment is supported by stronger state preschool policy and workforce demand, but affordability and staffing remain the main constraints.

Demand is still linked to maternal labor force participation and household income, while provider economics are heavily affected by labor costs, licensing requirements, and pricing pressure. The sector is increasingly shaped by public policy: states and legislators are trying to stabilize access through modernization, reauthorization, and quality standards while families report ongoing cost stress.

title: Nursing Care Facilities in the US
one_liner: US nursing care facilities are expanding into 2026 on demographics and post-acute demand, but labor scarcity and reimbursement pressure remain the key constraints.
overview: The U.S. nursing care market remains centered on short-stay rehabilitation plus long-stay support, with a national footprint of roughly 15,000 facilities and about 1.3 million people receiving care on any given day. Demand is propped up by policy-backed Medicaid dependence and post-acute flows, while operators are responding with workforce stabilization programs, service diversification, and tighter quality-performance differentiation.

title: Nutritionists & Dietitians
one_liner: A fragmented clinical-and-consulting nutrition sector in the U.S. with slow top-line growth, rising chronic-disease prevention demand, and faster shifts toward telehealth and food-system guidance channels.
overview: The industry remains a low-capex, labor-intensive professional-services market anchored in clinical nutrition counseling, meal planning, and diet-related disease management. IBIS baseline framing (2021 report) already described a mature but expanding market, and 2025–2026 public-health data show the demand context is still intact: adult obesity remains high at 40.3% (2021-2023 NHANES window), children’s obesity remains elevated, and private insurance coverage is broadly stable, sustaining referrals into clinical settings.
how_it_makes_money: Primary revenue comes from paid nutrition counseling and Medical Nutrition Therapy (MNT), hospital and outpatient clinic dietetic services, institutional/enterprise nutrition planning, school and long-term-care support programs, and private-pay wellness consultations; payer-based billing dominates clinical channels while private practice pricing dominates retail/consumer channels.

Baseline IBIS data show recovery from the 2020 COVID shock, and 2025–2026 official indicators point to continued demand: OSHA activity remained elevated in inspections and program guidance, and federal fatality/injury reporting indicates sustained need for prevention, training, and surveillance. The market now has a stronger split between direct service providers with physical clinic footprints and digital or on-demand compliance workflows, with large providers consolidating around value-added bundles (pre-employment health, return-to-work support, and risk management services).

title: Ocean & Coastal Transportation in the US
one_liner: U.S. ocean and coastal transport remains a two-speed market in 2026: freight remains volume-positive but price-sensitive, while cruise demand continues to expand.
overview: US liner trade and coastal freight remain essential to national logistics, with carriers reporting continued growth in 2025 imports/exports and strong cruise demand recovery in 2025. Freight conditions in 2025–2026 were mixed, with meaningful TEU/route growth shifts across coasts but sustained overcapacity pressure on container rates.

title: Office Furniture Rental

overview: Industry demand is tied to business formation, office-occupancy recovery, and willingness to avoid upfront capital in uncertain demand environments. IBIS-style baselines show modest long-run growth through 2026, while 2025–2026 demand signals from real-estate activity suggest a floor on softness as companies continue to reconfigure space rather than commit to long leases. In practice, the market is balancing two models: temporary rentals for immediate need and recurring rentals for scaling, contraction, or temporary expansions.

Commercial real-estate leasing rebounds are mostly in smaller transactions, pushing operators toward modular and scalable furniture solutions.
whats_growing: Private-flex and short-term workplace setup demand in sectors with variable staffing, including project-based and temporary operations.
Sublease activation for newly available office space, where furnished, quickly-occupied suites outcompete empty shell space.
Refurbishment and redeployment cycles (repair/recycle/remount) as utilization rises without equivalent new-build pressure.
whats_shrinking: Average office-lease size in 2025 remains below pre-pandemic norms, reducing one-off large interior-rental bundles.
Pure long-duration fixed-furniture commitments in uncertain sectors, where businesses prefer option-like rental terms.
Purely offline-only procurement versus omni-channel buying models in both product discovery and contract execution.
recent_developments: 2026-01-09: CoStar reported U.S. office leasing activity in 2025 rose 5% year over year to an estimated 410 million sq ft, with about 30,000 lease deals and average 3,500 sq ft lease size.
2025-Q2: NAIOP reported nationwide office vacancy at 11.8% and renewed quarterly net absorption (5.6 million sq ft in Q1), with hybrid-work intensity stabilizing.
2026-05-26: Irvine Company announced 2025 Flex+ leasing of about 2 million sq ft, with 415,000 sq ft leased in Q1 2026 and expanded partnerships including MillerKnoll and Williams Sonoma brands.
2026-07-02: BLS Employment Situation for June 2026 reported total nonfarm payroll growth of 57,000 and unemployment at 4.2%, supporting modest office staffing demand.
2026-? no month: CORT continues to emphasize furniture-as-a-service with short 1-, 3-, and 6-month lease terms, 3-5 day deployment and access-versus-ownership options for business customers.
outlook: Near-term growth is expected to stay modest but structurally supported by private-flex demand and ongoing office reconfiguration. The market likely benefits from continued workplace redesign and smaller, faster occupancy changes, while long-horizon expansion remains muted versus earlier pre-pandemic peaks; operators that combine inventory velocity, digital deal flow, and service reliability should gain share.
themes: Office space is moving from fixed occupancy to adaptive capacity, favoring shorter-cycle furniture contracts.
Furniture-as-a-service and flex-space partnerships are becoming an operating norm for landlords, startups, and portfolio operators.
Leasing markets are rebounding but still fragmented; smaller lease sizes imply modular, configurable rental bundles will dominate.
Procurement is shifting toward service-led offerings that combine desk/chair supply with transport, setup, and ongoing asset management, increasing differentiation beyond unit pricing.
one_sentence: The U.S. office-furniture rental segment is a low-growth but durable business-service market, benefiting from hybrid-work footprint churn, faster office reconfiguration, and cost-controlled access models.

title: Office Staffing & Temp Agencies in the US
one_liner: The U.S. office staffing and temporary help market is in a stabilization phase in 2025–2026, with demand holding, weaker first-quarter softness narrowing, and providers shifting toward higher-value, skill-specific talent solutions.
overview: U.S. office staffing and temp agencies supply on-demand talent for short-to-medium durations through legally employed agency workers, which lowers client administrative burden and provides flexibility in hiring cycles. In this period, core demand remained tied to macro hiring sentiment, unemployment conditions, sector-specific labor shortages, and enterprise workforce strategy. The industry is still influenced by cyclical volatility, but 2025–26 data show a slower pace of deterioration and earlier signs of recovery.

key_stats.market_size: 2026-07: temporary help services labor level about 2,505.0 thousand workers (CES temporary-help employment, month-on-month BLS CES table), implying roughly 2.5 million people engaged in this sector workforce stream.
key_stats.growth: 2026-07 is around 4.2% above 2025-07 in the same BLS temporary-help column; 2026-06 to 2026-07 showed a small positive move. 2026-04 average temporary-help weekly earnings were US$999.55 vs US$982.11 in 2026-03, and US$918.02 in 2025-05.

baseline_2022.market_size: US$235.9 billion industry revenue in 2022 (IBIS baseline projection)

how_it_makes_money: Providers earn primarily through temporary placement margins (bill rate minus paid hourly wage + payroll taxes/benefits handling), agency-marked payroll processing, markups on benefits and compliance administration, and direct/permanent-placement or specialist recruiting fees for higher-value roles.
cost_structure: Primary costs are workforce payroll and associated taxes/benefits, which dominate operating expense; a large share is also employee comp/compliance, recruiting sales overhead, and technology/ATS stack costs. Profitability is sensitive to wage inflation, utilization, and utilization efficiency by assignment and sector mix.
current_dynamics: Demand is seasonally sensitive but has become less fragile than in 2025: 2026 first-quarter seasonal weakness persisted but was smaller in pace, while quarterly staffing sales and payroll decline indicators narrowed. Temporary help remains structurally tied to labor shortages, especially where employers need elasticity, while clients increasingly demand faster match quality and compliance reliability. Wage growth in temp work remains elevated, helping workers but keeping staffing margins compressed.
whats_growing: Narrowing year-over-year declines in 1Q 2026 compared with 1Q 2025.
Higher-quality and specialized placements (IT, healthcare, finance, regulatory-heavy support roles).
Use of staffing as a flexible bridge during hiring uncertainty and budget discipline.
Employer spending on compliance-heavy workforce orchestration (payroll admin, tax handling, scheduling systems).
whats_shrinking: High-volume low-margin transactional placement in unstable demand periods.
Uncertainty-driven discretionary temporary hiring in discretionary office-operations roles.
Purely margin-accretion models relying on low-wage, high-turnover segments without efficiency gains.
recent_developments: 2026-06-25: ASA reported 1Q 2026 staffing employment fell 7.5% (154,000 jobs) versus 4Q 2025, but the 1Q year-over-year decline narrowed to 4.6% (improved from 10.8% in 1Q 2025).

2026-06-25: ASA reported 1Q 2026 staffing sales fell 4.3% versus 4Q 2025 to US$27.6 billion, while the year-over-year decline narrowed to 1.6%, the smallest first-quarter sequential deterioration since 2022.
2026-03-30: ASA reported 4Q 2025 staffing sales improved 2.6% from 3Q to US$29.9 billion and temporary/contract employment rose by 65,000 workers.
2025-12-29: ASA 3Q 2025 data showed slight staffing-employment increase quarter-to-quarter but sales down 1.3%.
2026-07: BLS CES temporary-help services labor remained above mid-2025 levels, with the monthly temporary-help indicator higher than July 2025.
outlook: The market is likely to remain in a soft-growth recovery mode through 2026: demand should hold where employers need workforce flexibility, with upside if wage and inflation pressures cool and if hiring confidence improves through Q2–Q3. Major players are expected to prioritize productivity, sector specialization, and pricing discipline over pure volume growth.
themes: Seasonal volatility persisting, but downside momentum flattening.
Rising wage and labor-cost pressure compressing margins.
Shift from pure volume staffing to skill-intense and compliance-sensitive placements.
More embedded technology in sourcing, onboarding, and assignment matching.
Healthcare, finance, and operations support remain key demand pockets.
one_sentence: Temporary workforce demand in the US stabilized through 2025–2026 as seasonal first-quarter declines moderated, while wage pressure and client cost scrutiny kept near-term growth uneven.
